robert.etyRaw: From {{der|en|xno|Robert}}, from the Old {{der|en|frk|-}} cognate of {{cog|goh|Hrodperht|}} (normalised form: {{m|goh|Ruodberht|}}), from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Hrōþiberht}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Hrōþiberhtaz|lit=shining glory}}. {{doublet|en|Rupert}}.

michael.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Michael}}, from {{der|en|fro|Michel}}, {{der|en|ang|Michahel}}, from their source {{der|en|la|Michaēl,Michāhēl}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μιχαήλ|Μῐχᾱήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|מִיכָאֵל|tr=mîḵāʾēl|lit=who is like God?}}. {{dbt|en|Miguel|Mikhail}}.

james.etyRaw: The English New Testament form of [[Jacob]], from {{der|en|enm|James}}, from {{der|en|fro|James}}, from {{der|en|la-vul|Iācōmus}}, spoken and altered pronunciation of {{der|en|la|Iācōbus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰάκωβος|}}, from {{m|grc|Ἰακώβ|}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יַעֲקֹב|tr=yaʿăqōḇ|lit=May He Heel}}, from the [[third-person singular]] [[masculine]] [[imperfective]] form of the [[Semitic]] verb "to heel" (with various meanings), in turn from {{m|he|עָקֵב|tr=ʿāqēḇ|t=heel of the foot}}. {{doublet|en|Jacques|Jacob|Iago|Jago|Yago|Hamish|Seamus|Tiago|Santiago|Yaakov}}. In reference to the Ecuadorian island, a modification of the earlier name {{m|en|Duke of York's Island}} after its eponymous duke's coronation as {{w|James II of England|James II}} of [[England]]. See {{cog|oc|Jacme}} for an intermediary between {{der|en|fro|James}} and {{cog|ca|Jaume}}.

john.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|John}}, {{m|enm|Johan}}, {{m|enm|Johannes}}, from {{der|en|xno|Jehan}}, {{m|fro|Johan}}, and also {{der|en|ang|Iohannes}}, both from {{der|en|la-lat|Iōhannēs}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Iōannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yôḥānān}}, perhaps contracted from a former {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן||God is gracious|tr=Yəhōḥānān}}. {{doublet|en|Jack|Jon|Johan|Johann|Johannes|Jean|Sean|Shane|Shaun|Ian|Ivan|Evan|Juan|Giovanni|Yahya}}.

william.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|William}}, from {{der|en|xno|Willame}}<!--many variants exist-->, from {{der|en|goh|Willahelm}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Wiljahelmaz}} (> {{cog|la|Gulielmus}}), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*wiljô||will}} + {{m|gem-pro|*helmaz||helmet}}, ultimately from the {{der|en|ine-pro|-}} roots {{m|ine-pro|*welh₁-||to choose, wish, want}} and {{m|ine-pro|*ḱel-||to cover, conceal, save}} respectively. Cognate with {{cog|nl|Willem}}, {{cog|de|Wilhelm}}, etc.; cognate borrowings outside of Germanic include {{dbt|en|Guillaume|Guillermo|notext=1}}.

mary.etyRaw: , {{circa2|1650|short=1}})]] From {{inh|en|enm|Marie}}, from {{der|en|fro|Marie}}, from {{der|en|la|Maria}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μαρία}}, {{m|grc|Μαριάμ}}, from {{der|en|arc|מַרְיָם|tr=maryām}} or {{der|en|hbo|מִרְיָם|tr=miryām}}, of uncertain meaning (see the Hebrew entry for more). {{doublet|en|Miriam|Marie|Maria|Mariah}}.

joseph.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Ioseph}}, ultimately from {{der|en|hbo|יוֹסֵף|tr=Yoséf|lit=(God) shall add}}; a son of Jacob. {{dbt|en|Yusuf}}. {{senseno|en|one whose chastity is above temptation|t=one whose chastity is above temptation|cap=1}} is a reference to the story of Joseph and [[Potiphar]]'s wife in [[w:Vayeshev|Genesis 39]].

richard.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Rycharde}}, from {{der|en|fro|Richard}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Richardus,Ricohardus}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Rīkahard}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Rīkaharduz}}, a construction of {{com|gem-pro|*rīks|t1=king, ruler|*harduz|t2=hard, brave|nocat=1}}. Cognate with {{cog|goh|Rīcohard|t=Richard}}. Partially related to {{m|en|rich}}. A hypothetical Old English equivalent {{m|ang||*Rī‌ċheard}} would also yield an identical "Richard" in Modern English, though it is unknown if the Old English equivalent existed.

charles.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fr|Charles}}, from {{der|en|fro|Charles}}, {{m|fro|Carles}}, from {{der|en|la|Carolus}}, from and also reinfluenced by {{der|en|frk|-}} and {{der|en|goh|Karl}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*karilaz|*karilaz|t=free man}}; compare the English word {{m|en|churl}} and the {{cog|de|Kerl}}. In reference to the Ecuadorian island, a clipping of the original name {{m|en|King Charles's Island}}, granted in honor of {{w|Charles II of England|Charles II}} of [[England]].

christopher.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la-lat|Christophorus}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Χρῑστόφορος||[[carrier]] of [[Christ]]}}, from {{der|en|grc|Χριστός||[[Christ]]}} + {{m|grc|φόρος||[[carrier]], [[bearer]]}}, from {{m|grc|φέρω|φέρειν|to [[carry]], to [[bear]]}} + {{m|grc|-ος||[[-er]]: ''[[form]]ing [[agent noun]]s''}}, from the legend of [[Saint Christopher]] carrying the infant Jesus across a river.

thomas.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Thomas}}, from {{der|en|la|Thōmās|g=m}} (as in the Vulgate), from {{der|en|grc|Θωμᾶς|g=m}}, the Biblical Greek transcription of {{der|en|arc|תאומא}} or {{m|arc|תאמא||twin}}, the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles. In the gospel of John (11:16, 20:24), the Aramaic nickname is also translated into Greek, as {{m|grc|δίδυμος|g=m}}. Used as a given name since the Middle Ages, e.g. {{w|Thomas the Presbyter}} (7th century), {{w|Thomas the Slav}} (8th century), {{w|Thomas of Bayeux}} (died 1100). {{sense|infidel or doubter}} In reference to the doubting Apostle.

elizabeth.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Elizabeth}}, from the {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ|}}, a transliteration of the Old Testament {{der|en|hbo|אלישבע||my [[God]] is an oath|tr=ʔĕlîšeḇaʕ}}. See {{m|en|El}} and {{m|he|שבועה}}. {{doublet|en|Elisheba|Isabel}}.

daniel.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Daniel}}, {{m|enm|Daniell}}, from {{der|en|grc|Δᾱνῑήλ}}, from {{der|en|he|דָּנִיֵּאל|tr=daniyél|lit=God is my judge}}, name borne from the prophet whose story is told in the Book of Daniel.<ref>''Oxford Names Companion''</ref>

matthew.etyRaw: From earlier {{m|en|Matheu}}, from {{der|en|fro|Mathieu}}, from {{der|en|la|Matthaeus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ματθαῖος}}, from {{der|en|arc|מַתַּי|tr=mattay}}. Compare {{cog|he|מַתִּתְיָהוּ|tr=mattiṯyāhū|sc=Hebr|lit=gift of the Lord}}. {{dbt|en|Mattathias}}.

patricia.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|la|patricia||noble}}; later also seen as the feminine form of the saint's name [[Patrick]].

george.etyRaw: Name of an early saint, from {{inh|en|enm|George}}, from {{der|en|la|Geōrgius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Γεώργῐος}}, from {{m|grc|γεωργός||farmer, earth worker}}, from {{m|grc|γῆ||earth}} (combining form {{m|grc||γεω-}}) + {{m|grc|ἔργον||work}} {{doublet|en|Jorge|Geevarghese}}. The aircraft autopilot sense is probably from George DeBeeson, who patented an early (1931) autopilot system, and/or a reference to the expression {{m|en|let George do it}}. The Pullman porter sense derives from {{w|George Pullman}}, who hired Black people to staff his [[sleeping car]]s, and the patrons of the service seeing the Black people as servants of George Porter, much like how a slave was named after the master.

anthony.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Antōnius}}, name of a Roman gens (with excrescent -h- suggested by an unetymological association with {{noncog|grc|ἄνθος||flower}}). The Roman clan name is of uncertain etymology, but is not Greek or Hebrew; most likely of {{der|en|ett|-}} origin, possibly derived from Ani, the Etruscan god of the sky. {{doublet|en|Antoine}}.

jennifer.etyRaw: From {{der|en|kw|Gweniver}}, from {{der|en|cnx|Gwynnever}} (cognate with {{cog|cy|Gwenhwyfar}}), from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*Gwɨnnohuɨβar}}<!--, equivalent to ''[[gwen]]'', meaning ''fair, white'', and [g]''[[hwyf]]''[ar], meaning ''smooth''-->. {{doublet|en|Guinevere}}. Compare {{cog|ga|Fionnabhair}}, which may be cognate. The {{IPAchar|/d͡ʒ/}} consonantism is due to Anglo-Norman influence; compare {{cog|fro|Genievre}} {{IPAchar|/d͡ʒəˈniɛ̯vɾə/|/d͡ʒəˈnjɛvɾə/}}.

linda.etyRaw: Latinised short form of {{der|en|gem}} compound names ending in {{m|de|-lind}}, {{m|de|-linde|t=tender, soft}} (English {{m|en|-inda}}), such as {{m|de|Sieglinde}} and {{m|de|Dietlinde}}, and earlier names such as {{cog|goh|Irmilinda}} and {{cog|odt|Frithelind|}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*linþaz|t=gentle, mild}}, whence also {{cog|ang|līþe|t=gentle, mild, pliable, limber}} ({{cog|en|lithe}}). Later misassociated with unrelated {{noncog|es|linda|t=beautiful}}. The name became known through 19th century literature and the opera ''Linda di Chamounix'' (1842). More at {{l|en|lithe}}. The coordination language is {{named-after|en|Linda Lovelace|wplink==|nocap=1}}, a reference to the programming language [[Ada]], itself named after {{w|Ada Lovelace}}.

barbara.etyRaw: * From {{der|en|la|Barbara}}, the name of {{w|Saint Barbara}}, feminine form of {{m|la|barbarus}}, from {{der|en|grc|βάρβαρος|t=strange, foreign}}. {{doublet|en|Varvara}}. * {{sense|logic}} From the given name; chosen because it has three A's in it representing universal affirmatives.

donald.etyRaw: Name of Scottish kings and an early saint, from {{bor|en|gd|Dòmhnall}} and reinforced by {{der|en|la-med|Donvaldus}} ~ {{m|la-med|Donaldus}}, from {{der|en|sga|Domnall}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*Dubnowalos|t=prince / chief of the world}}. {{doublet|en|Domhnall}}.

mark.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Mark}}, from the {{der|en|la|-}} {{m|en|praenomen}} (i.e. {{l|en|first name}}) {{m|la|Mārcus}}, derived from {{m|la|Mārs}}, the Roman god of war, originally {{m|la|Māvors}}, from {{der|en|itc-pro|*Māwortis}}.

edward.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Edward}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ēadweard}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Audawardu}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*Audawarduz}}, corresponding to {{m|en|ed||wealth, riches}} + {{m|en|ward||ward, guard}}, {{doublet|en|Eduard|nocap=y}}.

steven.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Stevene}}, {{m|enm|Steven}}, from {{der|en|xno|Estievne}}, {{m|xno|Estievene}}, from {{der|en|la|Stephanus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Στέφανος}}, from {{m|grc|στέφανος||crown, wreath}}, from {{m|grc|στέφω||to put round, to surround}}.

kenneth.etyRaw: Anglicized form of two {{der|en|cel-gae|-}} names, {{der|en|sga|Cináed}}, the name of Scottish kings derived from {{der|en|xpi|*ᚉᚔᚅᚔᚑᚇ|tr=Ciniod}}, and the saint's name {{m|sga|Cainnech|lit=handsome}} (modern {{cog|gd|Coinneach}}), as in the surname [[Mackenzie]].

margaret.etyRaw: From the name of 3rd century Saint [[w:Margaret the Virgin|Margaret the Virgin]], from {{inh|en|enm|Margaret}}, from {{der|en|fro|Margaret}} ({{cog|fr|Marguerite}}), from {{der|en|la|Margarita}}, from {{der|en|grc|μαργαρίτης||pearl}}, ultimately from an [[Indo-Iranian]] source. The same source, through folk etymology, has produced {{cog|ang|meregrot||pearl|lit=stone or pebble of the sea}}, related to {{cog|osx|merigrita}}, {{m|osx|merigriota||pearl}}, {{cog|goh|merigrioz}}, equivalent to {{prefix|en|mer|groat|nocat=1}}.

joshua.etyRaw: From {{der|en|hbo|יְהוֹשֻׁעַ|tr=Yehoshúa'}}, perhaps from {{m|he|הוֹשֵׁעַ|tr=Hoshéa'}} with addition of {{m|he|יהוה|tr=YHWH|t=Yahweh}}, thus meaning "Yahweh is salvation". See {{m|he|הוֹשִׁיעַ||tr=hoshía'|to save}}. By cognate a direct equivalent to {{m|en|Jesus}} via {{cog|la|Iēsūs}} and {{cog|grc|Ἰησοῦς}} from {{cog|arc|יֵשׁוּע|tr=Yēšū́ʿ}}, akin to {{cog|he|יֵשׁוּעַ|tr=Yeshúa'}}, a variant of ''Yehoshúa<nowiki>'</nowiki>''. The Greek [[Septuagint]] translation of the [[Hebrew Bible]] and the Greek [[New Testament]] consistently render the two Hebrew names ''Yehoshúa<nowiki>'</nowiki>'' (whence ''Joshua'') and ''Yeshúa<nowiki>'</nowiki>'' (whence {{m|en|Jeshua}}) into [[w:Koine Greek|Koine Greek]] as ''Iēsoûs'' (whence ''Jesus'').

kevin.etyRaw: Name of a seventh-century Irish saint, from {{der|en|ga|Caoimhghin}} or {{m|ga|Caoimhín}}, from {{der|en|sga|Cóemgen|lit=dear birth/person}}. It first became popular outside Ireland in the mid-twentieth century.

susan.etyRaw: English form of the biblical {{m|en|Susanna}}, from {{cog|hbo|שׁוֹשַׁנָּה||tr=šōšannā|lily}}, ultimately from {{der|en|egy|{{egy-h|z:S:n-M9}}|tr={{l|egy|zšn}}}}.

sarah.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|hbo|שָׂרָה|tr=śārâ|t=lady, princess}}, from {{w|Sarah|the Biblical figure}} originally named [[Sarai]] ({{m|he|שָׂרָי|tr=śārāy|lit=masters, princes}}).

ronald.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{bor|en|gd|Raghnall}}, itself derived from {{der|en|non|Rǫgnvaldr}}, from {{m|non|rǫgn||advice}} + {{m|non|valdr||power}}, later partly merged with the Continental Germanic equivalent [[Reynold]].

jason.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|grc|Ἰάσων|}}, from {{m|grc|ἰάομαι||I heal}}. The Jason mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 17:5-9, Romans 16:21) is probably a Greek rendering of [[Joshua]].

jessica.etyRaw: First used by William Shakespeare in ''{{w|Merchant of Venice}}'' in the early 17th century, probably from {{der|en|he|יִסְכָּה|tr=yiská|5=Iscah in Genesis 11:29, Jescha in the Wycliffe version}}, a proper name meaning "he will see/behold/look for", the 3ms imperfect form of a verb ultimately {{he-root|ס|כ|ה|tr=s-k-h|nocap=1}},<ref name="klein445">{{R:CEDHL|445}}</ref> itself an alternative form of the root {{m|he|שׂ־כ־ה|tr=ś-k-h}}, both of which mean "to see, behold, look for".<ref name="klein656">{{R:CEDHL|656}}</ref> * By folk etymology seen as an elaborate form of {{l|en|Jessie}}, from {{l|en|Jane}}.

karen.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|da|Karen}}, a vernacular form of ''[[Catherine]]'' that arose in medieval Denmark. The sense "middle-aged woman" comes from the popularity of the name among [[baby boomer]]s and [[Gen-Xer]]s. The derogatory usage was popularized via [[African-American Vernacular English]].<ref>{{cite-web|en |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-53588201 |publisher={{w|BBC}} |work=BBC News |date=2020-07-31 |accessdate=2020-07-30 |last=Nagesh |first=Ashitha |title=What exactly is a 'Karen' and where did the meme come from? |passage=Although its exact origins are uncertain, the meme became popular a few years ago as a way for people of colour, particularly black Americans, to satirise the class-based and racially charged hostility they often face.}}</ref>

jacob.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Iacob}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Iācōbus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰάκωβος}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יַעֲקֹב|tr=yaʿăqōḇ|lit=May He Heel}}, from the [[third-person singular]] [[masculine]] [[imperfective]] form of the [[Semitic]] verb "to heel" (with various meanings), in turn from {{m|he|עָקֵב|tr=ʿāqēḇ|t=heel of the foot}}. {{dbt|en|James|Yaakov|Yakub}}.

lisa.etyRaw: Diminutive of [[Elisabeth]] in several European languages. The computer is named after {{w|Lisa Brennan-Jobs}}, officially explained as an acronym for “Locally Integrated Software Architecture”.

frank.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Frank}}, partially from {{inh|en|ang|Franca||a Frank}}; and partially from {{der|en|fro|Franc}}, and/or {{der|en|la|Francus||a Frank}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Franko||a Frank}}; both maybe from {{der|en|gem-pro|*frankô||javelin}}. Cognate with {{cog|goh|Franko||a Frank}}, {{cog|ang|franca||spear, javelin}}. Compare {{m|en|Saxon}}, ultimately a derivative of {{m+|gem-pro|*sahsą||knife, dagger}}.<ref>{{R:OED Online|entry=Frank|id=74206|date=July 2021}}</ref> {{doublet|en|franc|frank|farang}}.

gary.etyRaw: Medieval short form of {{der|en|gem|-}} compound names beginning with ''gari'' or ''geri'' ("spear"), such as {{m|en|Gerard}}, {{m|en|Garrett}}, {{m|en|Gerald}}{{,}} or {{m|en|Gerbert}}. Cognate with the Scottish and {{cog|ga|-}} name {{m|en|Garaidh}}. Sometimes also a short form of {{m|en|Gareth}}. The popularity of the given name in the 20th century is due to the {{person|Q93957}}, whose stage name was invented by his agent, a native of {{w|Gary, Indiana}}.

anna.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} both directly and via numerous other languages, chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[Vulgate]] in reference to {{w|Anne the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα}} in the [[New Testament]], from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. As a city in Illinois, named for Anna Davie, wife of one of the initial settlers. {{doublet|en|Ann|Anne|Ana|Hannah}}.

emily.etyRaw: English form of {{uder|en|la|Aemilia}}, a gens name from {{m|la|aemulus||[[rival]], [[emulator]]}}.

eric.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Eric}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Eoric}}, from {{der|en|non|Eirríkr}}, {{m|non|Eiríkr|pos=from {{af|non|ei|t1=always, eternal|pos1=see {{m|en|aye}}|ríkr|t2=ruler|nocat=1}}}}, or from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Aizarīkijaz|pos=from {{af|gem-pro|*aizō|t1=honor|*rīkijaz|t2=ruler|nocat=1}}}}. Less likely from {{af|non|einn|t1=sole, alone|ríkr|t2=ruler|nocat=1}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*rīks|t=king|pos=cognate to {{cog|la|rēx}} and {{cog|cel-gau|*rīx}}}}. The name was in use in Anglo-Saxon Britain, reinforced by Scandinavian settlers before the Norman Conquest. Compare {{cog|da|Erik}}, {{cog|de|Erich}}. Possible {{doublet|en|Euric|nocap=1}}.

sandra.etyRaw: A short form of {{m|en|Alexandra}} and, less often, of {{m|en|Cassandra}}.

ashley.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|*Æsċlēah}}, composed of {{m|ang|æsċ|t=[[ash]] tree}} + {{m|ang|lēah|t=[[wood]], [[clearing]]}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|ash|alt1=Ash|-leigh|alt2=-ley}}.

jonathan.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|he|יְהוֹנָתָן|tr=yəhōnāṯān}}, {{m|he|יוֹנָתָן|tr=yōnāṯān|lit=God has given}}, apparently with influence from {{ncog|arc}}.

stephen.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Stephanus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Στέφανος}}, from {{m|grc|στέφανος||crown, wreath}}, from {{m|grc|στέφω||to put round, to surround}}. From {{m|ine-pro|*stegʷʰ-||to enlace}} + {{m|grc|-νος|pos=suffix forming an adjective or noun}} from {{der|en|ine-pro|*-nós|pos=suffix forming a verbal adjective from a verb stem}}.

ruth.etyRaw: From Ruth the [[Moabite]], {{der|en|he|רות}}, of uncertain origin, possibly meaning "[[companion]]". Also associated with the English noun {{m|en|ruth||compassion}} by Puritans.

donna.etyRaw: A 19th-century invention from the {{der|en|it|-}} noun {{m|it|donna}}; also interpreted as a feminine form of [[Donald]].

benjamin.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la-lat|Benjamin}}, from {{der|en|grc|Βενιαμίν}}, from {{der|en|hbo|בִּנְיָמִין|tr=binyamīn|lit=son of the right/south or son of days}}. Authorities differ on the meaning of the original Hebrew. Philo of Alexandria, the Samaritan Pentateuch ''The Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs'' and ''Midrash Leḳaḥ-Ṭob'' understand יָמִין to mean "days" (a meaning attested in ''Daniel 12:13'') understanding the name to mean "son of days (i.e. old age)" (compare to the direct translations into {{cog|ar|'''بِنْ يَومِين'''}} ('''bin yawmīn''') "son of the days" and {{cog|ar|'''بِنْ يَمِين'''}} "son of the right hand"), a formula paraphrased in ''Genesis 40:22'' where Benjamin is described as a child of Jacob's old age. Rashi in his commentary on ''Genesis'' also gives this as a possible meaning but favors an understanding of יָמִין to mean "right" in the sense of "the south", noting that Benjamin was the only son of Jacob born in the south. Jerome understood the name to mean "son of the right hand" and Gesenius speculated that this expression might have meant "son of good fortune".

carol.etyRaw: Shortened from {{m|en|Caroline}}. Associated by [[folk etymology]] with the English noun {{m|en|carol}}.

michelle.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Michelle}}, feminine form of {{der|en|fr|Michel||Michael}}, {{der|en|he|מִיכָאֵל||who is like God?|tr=mikhaél}}. {{doublet|en|Michaela}}.

samuel.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Samuēl}}, from {{der|en|grc|Σαμουήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|שְׁמוּאֵל|tr=šəmûʾēl|lit='God has set' or 'God has placed'}}.<ref>{{R:Strong's|H|410}}</ref><ref>{{R:Strong's|H|7760}}</ref> Taken to mean a contraction of popular folk etymology {{l|he|שְׁאִלְתִּיו מֵאֵל|gloss=I have asked/borrowed him from God}} (Modern: Šəʾīltīv mēʾĒl, Tiberian: Šĭʾīltīw mēʾĒl) by way of {{l|he|שָׁאוּל מֵאֵל|gloss=asked/borrowed from God}}<ref>{{R:Strong's|H|7592}}</ref> from [https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+samuel+1%3A20&version=NIV 1 Samuel 1:20].<ref>{{cite-web |title=Radak on Genesis 5:29:1 |url=https://www.sefaria.org/Radak_on_Genesis.5.29?lang=bi |site=Sefaria|year=1842|publisher=A. Schmid}}</ref>

laura.etyRaw: From Late {{der|en|la|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Laura}}, from the feminine form of {{m|la|laurus||laurel tree}}. A post-classical name made famous by [[Petrarch]]'s sonnets to Laura in the fourteenth century.

justin.etyRaw: Name of early saints, {{der|en|la|Iūstīnus}}, from {{m|la|Iūstus}} + {{m|la|-īnus}}, from {{m|la|iūstus||just}}.

amanda.etyRaw: {{der+|en|la|Amanda}}, feminine form of the saint's name {{taxfmt|Amandus|genus}}, from {{m|la|amandus}}, future passive participle of {{m|la|amāre||to love}}: thus meaning "who/which is to be loved". Taken into regular use as an English given name from 18th-century literature. {{doublet|en|Aimee}}.

raymond.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Raimund}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Raginmund}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Raginamunduz}}, composed of {{af|gem-pro|*raginą|t1=advice|*mundō|t2=protection|nocat=1}}. Compare the first element in {{m|en|Reginald}}, {{m|en|Reynold}}, {{m|en|Ronald}}; the second element can be found in cognates {{m|en|Edmund}}, {{m|en|Sigmund}}, {{m|en|Osmond}}.

emma.etyRaw: Brought to England by the [[Norman]]s; short form of compound given names beginning with a [[Frankish]] [[prototheme]] ''[[Ermin-]]'' or ''[[Irmin-]]'' "entire", from {{der|en|gem-pro|*ermunaz}}.

henry.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Henry}}, from {{der|en|fro|-}} (and {{der|en|xno|-}}) {{m|fro|Henri}}, from {{der|en|frk||*Haimrik}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Haimarīks}}. Cognate with {{cog|de|Heinrich}}, {{cog|nl|Hendrik}}, {{cog|et|Hendrik}}, and {{cog|non|Heimríkr}} ({{cog|da|Henrik}}).

jack.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Jackin}}, {{m|enm|Jankyn}}, a popular pet form of {{m|enm|John}}; rarely also an anglicized form of {{der|en|fr|Jacques}} (equivalent of [[Jacob]] and [[James]]). It can be also used as nickname for [[Jacob]]. Though the name was originally a pet form, it has become more of an independent name. Equivalent to {{m|en|John}} + {{m|en|-kin}}, {{m|en|Jake}} or {{m|en|Jacques}}.  See also {{cog|frm|Hennequin}}, {{m|frm|Jannequin}} and {{cog|dum|Janneken}}.

melissa.etyRaw: From {{der|en|grc|μέλισσα||bee, honey, or honeybee}}. In Ireland it is sometimes used as a feminine form of the Gaelic male name {{m|ga|Maol Íosa|lit=servant of Jesus}}.

rebecca.etyRaw: The [[Vulgate]] ({{bor|en|la|-}}) form of biblical {{m|en|Rebekah}}, from {{der|en|he|רִבְקָה||enchantingly beautiful, captivating, snare|tr=Rivka}}.

stephanie.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Stéphanie}}. The standard English feminine form of {{m|en|Stephen}}. {{doublet|en|Stephania}}.

alexander.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|la|Alexander}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος}}, from {{m|grc|ἀλέξω||to defend}} + {{m|grc||ἀνδρ-}}, the stem of {{m|grc|ἀνήρ||man}}. {{doublet|en|Alastair|Alejandro|Iskandar|Sikandar|Alessandro|Alexandre}}.

kathleen.etyRaw: Anglicization of {{m|ga|Caitlín}}, an {{der|en|ga|-}} equivalent of the English [[Catherine]].

gregory.etyRaw: Via {{der|en|la|Grēgorius}}, from post-classical {{der|en|grc|Γρηγόριος|t=watchful, vigilant}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἐγείρω|t=awaken, arouse}}.

amy.etyRaw: Anglicized form of {{der|en|fro|Amee}} (modern French [[Aimée]]), which was both a nickname and a form of the {{der|en|la|-}} name {{m|la|Amata||beloved}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of Given Names.Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>

cynthia.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|la|Cynthia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κυνθία}}, feminine of {{m|grc|Κύνθιος||[[Cynthian]] (of or pertaining to Mount [[Cynthus]], a mountain of [[Delos]], celebrated as the birthplace of [[Apollo]] and [[Artemis]])}}.

shirley.etyRaw: English place name from {{der|en|ang|sċīr||county}} + {{m|ang|lēah||meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|shire|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}. More at {{m|en|shire}}, {{m|en|leigh}}.

patrick.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Patrick}}, from {{der|en|la|Patricius|t=patrician}}, the name of an early Irish saint. {{dbt|en|Paddy}}.

angela.etyRaw: Feminine form of Church {{der|en|la|Angelus}}, from {{der|en|grc|ἄγγελος||messenger, angel}}.

catherine.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Catherine}}, from {{der|en|grc|Αἰκατερίνη}}, {{m|grc|*Ἑκατερίνη}}, of debated meaning, possibly from {{m|grc|ἑκάτερος||each of the two}}, or from the name of the goddess [[Hecate]]. The {{glossary|apheresis}} of the first syllable as well as the spelling with ⟨th⟩ in Latin languages, German and English, is due to a [[folk etymology]], dating from Roman times, which associated the name with the Ancient Greek {{m|grc|καθαρός||pure}}. The name belonged to a 4th-century [[saint]] and [[martyr]] from [[Alexandria]] who was tortured on the wheel from where the term [[Catherine wheel]] originates.

virginia.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Virginia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Virginius}} or {{m|la|Verginius}}, a Roman family name, possibly identical with [[Vergilius]]. The state/colony was named for {{w|Elizabeth I}} as the Virgin Queen, equivalent to {{af|en|virgin|-ia|id2=place}}.

evelyn.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|-}} forms of the {{der|en|fro|-}} female name {{m|fro|Aveline}}, diminutive of the {{der|en|gem|-}} root {{m|gem-pro|*avi-}}, of uncertain meaning, possibly “desired, wished for“ (compare {{cog|la|aveo|avēre}}, "to wish for") or ''aval'' “strength”. By {{glossary|folk etymology}} also misunderstood as a diminutive of the feminine given name {{m|en|Eve}}, q.v. {{doublet|en|Eileen}}. Also compare {{m|en|Ava}}.

walter.etyRaw: A {{der|en|gem}} name, from {{inh|en|enm|Walter}}, from {{der|en|fro-nor|Waltier}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Waltheri}} (compare {{cog|goh|Waltheri}}, which see for more details), from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Waldahari}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*Waldaharjaz}}, from {{com|gem-pro|*waldą|t1=ruler|*harjaz|t2=army, host|nocat=1}}. Related to {{cog|ang|Waldhere}}. Compare {{m|en|herald}} and {{m|en|Harold}}, in which these elements are reversed.

dennis.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Denis}}, from {{der|en|fro|-}} saint's name {{m|fro|Denis}}, brought to England by Normans; from Latin {{m|la|Dionysius}}, a masculine name literally meaning “follower of (the wine god) [[Dionysus]]”.

brenda.etyRaw: Possibly from {{der|en|non|brandr||sword}}; by [[folk etymology]] seen as a feminine form of {{m|en|Brendan}}.<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press.2001.</ref> Its use as a nickname for Queen Elizabeth II originated in ''[[w:Private Eye|Private Eye]]'' in reaction to a perceived attempt by the royals to appear less distant and upper class.<ref>1997, October 5, Andrew Sullivan, "[http://www.nytimes.com/1997/10/05/books/god-help-the-queen.html God Help the Queen]", ''The New York Times''.</ref>

aaron.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Aaron}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀαρών}}, from {{der|en|he|אַהֲרֹן||tr=ʾAhărōn}}, of unknown meaning, possibly meaning “[[bearer]] of [[martyr]]s”, or perhaps also, or instead, related to the Ancient Egyptian {{m|egy|[[ꜥḥꜣ]] [[rw]]||[[warrior]] [[lion]]}}, though it has been suggested to also mean “[[elevated]]”, “[[exalted]]” or “[[high]] [[mountain]]”. {{doublet|en|Harun}}.

pamela.etyRaw: Invented by Sir {{w|Philip Sidney}} for his pastoral poem ''{{w|The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia}}'' (c 1593). Seemingly created from scratch;<ref>Patrick Hanks, Kate Hardcastle, Flavia Hodges. ''A Dictionary of First Names'', Oxford University Press, 2006</ref> some imagine an analysis as {{cog|grc|πᾶς||all}} + {{m|grc|μέλι||honey}} but there is no evidence that this was intended.

olivia.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Olīva}}, an early saints’ name from {{m|la|olīva||olive; olive branch}}. First popularized by Shakespeare's ''{{w|Twelfth Night}}''.

janet.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Jane|et}}, q.v. Chiefly Scottish until the 19th century. {{doublet|en|Jeanette|Jeannette|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead}}.

harold.etyRaw: From a merger of {{inh|en|ang|Hereweald}} and {{inh|en|ang|Harold}} (itself from {{der|en|non|Haraldr}}),<ref name=BosworthToller>[https://bosworthtoller.com/18195 Bosworth, Joseph. “Harold.” In ''An Anglo-Saxon Dictionary Online'', edited by Thomas Northcote Toller, Christ Sean, and Ondřej Tichy. Prague: Faculty of Arts, Charles University, 2014.]</ref> both from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*Harjawaldaz}}, from {{com|gem-pro|*harjaz|*waldaz|t1=army|t2=ruler, authority|nocat=1}}. Related to {{m|en|Walter}}, which has the elements reversed. Cognate with {{cog|da,nn,sv|Harald}}, {{cog|fo,is|Haraldur}}.

martha.etyRaw: * From {{der|en|la|Martha}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μάρθα|}}, from {{der|en|arc|מָרְתָא|t=mistress|tr=mārtā}}, feminine of {{m|arc|מרא|tr=mārā}}. {{doublet|en|Marfa}}. * {{sense|humidity chamber}} From the use of {{w|Martha Stewart}}-branded storage closets in the construction of early units.

debra.etyRaw: A spelling variant of [[Deborah]] first used in the 20th century.

arthur.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|cel|cel-bry-pro|cel-pro|ine-pro}} From the name of the legendary king, from {{inh|en|enm|Arthure}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Arthurus}}, probably from {{der|en|wlm|-}} {{m|cy|arth|t=bear}}. Other suggestions include {{der|en|owl|arth||bear}} and {{m|owl|ur||man}}, or a Latinized ([[w:Romano-British culture|Romano-British]]) name; compare {{cog|la|Artorius}}, itself possibly of Etruscan origin, or more likely {{w|Messapic}}-Illyrian related to {{cog|sqj-pro|*artsa||bear}}.

marie.etyRaw: The {{bor|en|fr|Marie}}, equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}}; also an Early New English spelling of ''Mary'', from {{inh|en|enm|Marie}}. {{doublet|en|Mary}}.

jordan.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Iordanēs}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰορδάνης}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יַרְדֵּן|tr=yardén|t=Jordan (river)}}. {{doublet|en|Yarden}}. The area in Hong Kong is named after {{w|Jordan station}}, which is named after {{w|Jordan Road, Hong Kong|Jordan Road}}, which in turn is {{named-after|en|Sir John Jordan|wplink=John Jordan (diplomat)|nocap=1}}.

grace.etyRaw: From the noun {{m|en|grace}}, first used by Puritans in the 16th century. In Roman Catholic use it may refer to {{w|Our Lady of Graces}}, cognate with Italian [[Grazia]].

heather.etyRaw: From {{m|en|heather}}; the given name is one of the plant names taken up in the 19th century. The surname is habitational, also meaning someone living on a [[heath]].

joyce.etyRaw: Medieval ({{der|en|enm|-}}) given name from {{der|en|fro|Josse}}, name of a seventh century saint Latinized as {{m|la|Iodocus}}, from {{der|en|br|Iodoc}}, diminutive of {{m|br|iudh||lord}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*yowdos}}.<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Dictionary of Surnames. Oxford University Press 1988.</ref>

victoria.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Victōria}}, from {{m|la|victōria||victory}}. {{doublet|en|Vitória}}. The given name can also be analyzed as the male name {{suffix|en|Victor|ia|id2=female given name}}. {{cln|en|eponyms|terms suffixed with -ia}}<!-- not only placenames--> The places were named in honour of {{w|lang=en|Queen Victoria}} of Great Britain.

kyle.etyRaw: From several [[place]]s in [[Scotland]] and [[Northern Ireland]], derived from [[Gaelic]] ''[[caol]]'' (“[[narrows]]”).

albert.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|Æþelbeorht}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Aþalaberht}}, a compound of {{m|gem-pro|*aþalaz||noble}} + {{m|gem-pro|*berhtaz||bright, famous}}, or from {{der|en|fro|Albert}}, from {{der|en|la|Albertus}}, itself from the Germanic name. Regardless of the exact route, it is a {{doublet|en|Ethelbert|nocap=1}}. It became popular in 19th-century England due to Queen Victoria’s consort, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.

rose.etyRaw: * As an English, Scottish, {{der|en|fr|-}}, {{der|en|wa|-}}, {{der|en|da|-}}, Jewish ({{der|en|yi|רויז}}), and {{der|en|de|-}} surname, all from the noun {{m|en|rose}}. Also adapted from foreign forms of the same meaning such as {{der|en|hu|Rózsa}}, {{m|en|Rozsa}}, {{der|en|sk|Róža}}, {{der|en|cs|Roza}}, etc. Compare {{m|en|Larose}}. The surname may be matronymic, but more probably topographic from residence by rose bushes or the sign of a rose, or a nickname from rosy complexion. * Also as an English surname, from a {{der|en|nrf|-}} name of {{der|en|gem|-}} origins, likely made up of {{der|en|gem-pro|*hrod|t=fame}} and {{m|gem-pro|*heid|t=kind, sort, type}}, ultimately evolved from {{m|gem-pro|*hrōþiz}}. Introduced to England in the form Roese or Rohese. * As an English and Scottish surname, variant of {{m|en|Ross}}. * As a {{der|en|sl|-}} surname, Americanized or Italianized from {{m|en|Rože}}, from a short form of {{m|en|Erazem}} (from {{der|en|la|Erasmus}}), compare {{m|en|Rozman}}.

joan.etyRaw: A clipped or [[hypochoristic]] form of {{m|en|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}}. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

jean.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehane}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}}. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}. The unincorporated community in Nevada, originally named Goodsprings Junction, was renamed Jean on 28 June 1905 by postmaster George Arthur Fayle in honor of his wife.

christina.etyRaw: Name of an early martyr, shortened from {{der|en|la|Chrīstiāna||Christian (woman)}}. {{doublet|en|Kirsten}}.

lillian.etyRaw: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of [[Elizabeth]], but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin {{m|la|lilium||lily}}.

julia.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Iūlia}}, feminine form of the Roman gens name {{m|la|Iūlius}}. Further popularized by early Christian saints. {{doublet|en|Julie}}.

ann.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[Vulgate]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα||[[Anna]]}} in the [[New Testament]], from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. Occasionally reborrowed from languages who adopted the name from English. Very infrequently from {{bor|en|et|-}} abbreviation of {{m|et|Anna}} instead. {{doublet|en|Ana|Anna|Anne|Hannah}}.

hannah.etyRaw: From previous romanizations of {{der|en|he|חַנָּה|tr=Ḥannâ}}, chiefly for the mother of [[Samuel]], from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. As a Wren with the Royal Marines, after {{w|Hannah Snell}} (1723–1792) who disguised herself as a man to serve in the British military. {{doublet|en|Ann|Anne|Anna|Ana}}.

christian.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Cristien}}, from {{der|en|fro|chrestien}}, from {{der|en|la|Chrīstiānus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Χρῑστιᾱνός}}, from {{m|grc|Χρῑστός||Christ, anointed [one]}} + {{der|en|la|-}} suffix {{m|la|-ānus}}. The older form is {{m|en|Christen}}. {{doublet|en|cretin}}. {{surf|en|Christ|-ian}}.

joe.etyRaw: {{U|short form}} ([[diminutive]] form) of various names beginning with ''Jo...'', particularly the male names [[Joseph]] and, less often, [[Joel]], [[Josiah]] and [[Josias]]. The spelling {{m|en|Jo}} is used more often for diminutives of similar female names.

doris.etyRaw: From {{der|en|grc|Δωρίς}}. {{senseno|en|Q180589|pos=false|cap=1}} is owing to similarity to {{m|en|Boris}}.

carl.etyRaw: From {{der|en|gem|-}}, cognate with {{cog|en|Charles}}. * From {{bor|en|de|-}} and other north European {{m|de|Carl}} and {{m|de|Karl}}. * From {{der|en|la|Carolus}}.

charlotte.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Charlotte}} in the 17th century, a female diminutive form of {{m|fr|Charles}}, from {{der|en|gmh|Karl}}, which came from the Germanic {{m|gem-pro||*karlaz}}. The civil parish is named after {{w|Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz}} (1744-1818). {{coin|en|Samuel Holland|occ=surveyor|nat=British-Dutch}}.

mildred.etyRaw: From the name of an 8th-century English saint, {{inh|en|ang|Mildþrȳþ|pos=from {{af|ang|milde|t1=mild|þrȳþ|t2=strength|nocat=1}}}}.

roger.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Rogier|}}, from the {{der|en|frk|-}} equivalent of {{cog|ang|Hrōþgār}} (see [[w:Hroðgar|Hroðgar]]), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Hrōþigaizaz||fame-spear}}. Compare also {{l|en|Rutger}}.

austin.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Austin}}, from {{der|en|xno|Aostin}}, {{m|fro|Austin}}, similar to {{der|en|fro|Aostin, Austin}}, a popular variant of {{der|en|fro|Agustin}}, from {{der|en|la|Augustīnus}}, from {{m|la|Augustus|lit=majestic}}. {{dbt|en|Augustine}}.

megan.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|cy|Megan}}, cognate with {{cog|en|Margaret}}, ultimately from an [[Indo-Iranian]] source.

cheryl.etyRaw: Coined in the early 20th century, possibly a blend of {{m|en|Cherie}} or {{m|en|Cherry}} and {{m|en|Beryl}}. (See {{l|fr|cher}} for the etymology of Cherie.)

keith.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|cel}} * As a Scottish surname, from the placename in [[Moray]], Scotland, from {{der|en|gd|Cèith}}, meaning "wood" or "from the battleground," which is probably borrowed from {{der|en|xpi|*ᚉᚓᚈ|tr=cēt}} meaning "wood", or a forest, from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*koɨd}}.<ref>{{R:en:DFN}}</ref><ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref> * As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, from {{der|en|gmh|kit|t=sprout, offspring}} (compare {{m|gmh|kint}}).

sophia.etyRaw: Chiefly from {{bor|en|la|Sophia}}, from {{der|en|grc|Σοφία}}, from {{m|grc|σοφία||[[wisdom]]}}, especially in reference to {{w|Holy Wisdom|holy}} or {{w|sophia (wisdom)|divine wisdom}} under the influence of {{der|en|hbo|חוכמה|tr=khokhmá}}, to the early martyr {{w|Sophia of Rome|St. Sophia}}, and to many figures of European royalty and nobility. Also used as a [[calque]] for the many cognate forms, such as Italian {{m|it|Sofia}}, Ukrainian {{m|uk|Софі́я}}, Russian {{m|ru|Софи́я}}, Polish {{m|pl|Zofia}}, etc. {{dbt|en|Sofia}}.

dylan.etyRaw: From {{der|en|cy|-}} mythology; possibly from {{der|en|cel|-}} for "son of the sea" or "born from the ocean." Unrelated to the name {{m|en|Dillon}}, although the homophony may result in the two being considered variant spellings of the same name.

jacqueline.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Jacqueline}}, a feminine diminutive form of {{m|fr|Jacques|t=[[James]]}}, from {{der|en|he|יעקב|tr=ya'akóv|t=[[Jacob]]}}, from the root {{m|he|עקב|tr=‘akev|t=[[heel]]}}, because the biblical patriarch {{w|Jacob}} was born just behind {{w|Esau}}, and was grasping Esau’s heel in an effort to prevent him from being born first.

sean.etyRaw: Anglicised form of {{bor|en|ga|Seán}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehan}}, from {{der|en|la|Johannes}}, variant of {{m|la|Ioannes}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}. {{dbt|en|John|Jack|Johan|Johann|Johannes|Jean|Ian|Evan|Ivan|Shaun|Shane|Giovanni}}.

madison.etyRaw: Usually derived from [[Mathieson]] ({{m|en|Matthew}} + {{m|en|-son}}), occasionally from {{der|en|enm|Maddy||[[Maud]]}} + {{m|en|-son}}. <ref>P. H. Reaney and R. M. Wilson, ''A Dictionary of English Surnames'', Oxford University Press, 1997, page 293.</ref> In the movie ''Splash'', its use as a given name derives from Manhattan’s [[Madison Avenue]].

isabella.etyRaw: Latinate and Italian form of {{m|en|Isabel}}. The grape cultivar is popularly thought to have been discovered by a Mrs Isabella Gibbs of South Carolina in 1816.

teresa.etyRaw: First recorded as the name of a fourth-century Spanish saint. Of obscure origin; suggestions include [[Therasia]] or [[Thera]], ancient name of the [[Greek]] island [[Thira]].

gloria.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|gloria||glory}}, first used as a name in 19th-century literature.

ralph.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Radulf}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Rǣdwulf}} (also as {{m|ang|Raulf}}), from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Rādawulf}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*Rēdawulfaz}}. Reinforced by similar forms brought to England, e.g. {{cog|non|Ráðúlfr}}, then in the Norman form {{cog|fro|Radulf}}, {{m|fro|Radulph}}. For the sense relating to vomiting, see {{m|en|ralph}}.

abigail.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|he|אֲבִיגַיִל||Abigail|lit=my Father's joy” or “fountain of joy|tr=avigáyil}}.

roy.etyRaw: From various sources: * {{der|en|xno|roy|t=king}} a variant of {{der|en|fro|roi}}, from  {{der|en|la|rex|rēx, rēgem}} from  {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₃rḗǵs||ruler, king}}. {{doublet|en|Rey}}. * {{der|en|gd|ruadh|t=red, red-haired}} from {{der|en|sga|rúad}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*roudos}} from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₁rewdʰ-}}. * Anglicisation of {{bor|en|bn|রায়|pos=surname}}. {{dbt|en|Rai|rex|rajah}}.

gerald.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|gem-pro}} From {{der|en|fro|-}}, ultimately from {{der|en|frk|*gaiʀ||spear}} + {{m|frk|*wald||might, power}}. The name was brought to England by the [[Norman]]s. It survived in [[Ireland]], and was revived in the 19th century.

louis.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Louis}}, from {{der|en|frm|Loïs}}, {{m|frm|Loïc}}, &c., from {{der|en|fro|Looïs}}, {{m|fro|Luis}}, {{m|fro|Lodhuvigs}}, {{m|fro|Lodevis}}, {{m|fro|Lodhwig}}, &c., from {{der|en|la|Ludovicus}}, from {{m|la|Clodovicus}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Hlūdawīg}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*hlūdaz|t=loud; famous}} + {{m|gem-pro|*wīgą|t=battle}}. {{doublet|en|Lewis}} (which is inherited since the Middle Ages) and, more remotely, {{m|en|Aloysius}}, {{m|en|Luis}}, {{m|en|Ludwig}}, {{m|en|Luigi}}, and {{m|en|Clovis}}.

janice.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Jane}} under apparent influence from {{m|en|Alice}}, {{m|en|Bernice}}, {{m|en|Eunice}}, etc.,  from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}} and earlier use of {{m|en|Joan}} in the same role. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

theresa.etyRaw: First used in [[Spain]], supposedly derived from {{der|en|la|Thēra}}, from {{der|en|grc|Θήρᾱ}}, name of a city in Santorini, Greece.

bruce.etyRaw: From a Norman place name, [[w:Brix, Manche|Brix]], of disputed meaning.

gabriel.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Gabriel}}, from {{der|en|grc|Γαβρῑήλ}}, from {{der|en|he|גַּבְרִיאֵל|tr=gaḇrīʾḗl|t=God is my strong man}}, from {{m|he|גֶּבֶר|tr=géver|t=strong man, hero}} and {{m|he|אֵל|tr=ʾēl|t=God, deity}}, from {{der|en|sem-pro|*ʾil-}}. {{doublet|en|Jibril}}.

leslie.etyRaw: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally ''Lesslyn'', {{der|en|gd|[[lios]] [[cuileann]]|t=garden of hollies}}.

eugene.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Eugène}}, from {{der|en|la|Eugenius}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὐγένιος||well born}}, from {{suf|grc|εὖ|t1=good, well|γενής|t2=born a certain way|nocat=1}}. Parallel to {{m|en|eugenics}}. {{doublet|en|Yevgeny|Eugenius|Owen}}.

jane.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}} and earlier use of {{m|en|Joan}} in the same role. {{dbt|en|Gianna|Ivana|Jana|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

elijah.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|אליהו|tr=Eliyahu|lit=[[Yahweh]] is my god}}. {{doublet|en|Ilya|Iliya}}. Compare {{m|en|Joel}}. See also Arabic {{m|ar|إلياس}}.

natalie.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} form of the {{der|en|la-lat|-}} saint's name {{m|la|Natalia}}, from {{m|la|[[nātālis]] ([[diēs]])|t=birthday [of Christ], Christmas}}. {{doublet|en|Natalya}}.

ruby.etyRaw: The female name derives from {{m|en|ruby}} in the 19th century. The programming language was named after the gemstone.

denise.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|fr|Denise}}, from {{der|en|la|Dionȳsia|pos=feminine form of {{m|la|Dionȳsius}}, a male name of {{uder|en|grc|-}} origin meaning “follower of [[Dionysus]]”}}. Dionysus is the mythological Greek god of wine responsible for growth of the vines and the originator of winemaking. {{doublet|en|Dionysia}}.

diana.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la-lat|Diāna}}, short form of {{der|en|la|Dīāna}}, derived by [[syncope]] from {{der|en|itc-ola|Dīvāna}}, equivalent to {{suffix|la|dīvus|-āna|nocat=1}}; roughly akin to {{der|en|itc-pro|*deiwā|t=goddess}} + {{der|en|ine-pro|*-nós|*-néh₂}}. Originally an Old [[Italic]] [[divinity]] of [[light]] and the [[moon]]; later identified as the [[Roman]] counterpart to [[Greek]] goddess [[Artemis]]. Cognate of {{cog|grc-att|Διώνη}}, similarly [[syncopated]] from older {{cog|grc|Διϝωνη}}, whence via {{cog|la|Diōne}} is derived {{cog|en|Dione}} used in various ways across astronomy, chemistry, biology, and as a given name. From the same root {{cog|ine-pro|*dyúh₃onh₂-}} also potentially cognate to {{cog|en|June}} via {{cog|la|Iūnō|Jūnō}}.

alan.etyRaw: From {{der|en|obt|Alan}}, name of early {{der|en|br|-}} saints, of disputed origin and meaning; brought to England by [[Norman]]s.  It may have been the name of a Celtic deity, the brother of ''Bran'', {{cog|cy|Alawn}}, {{m|cy|Alun}}. As an early Irish name, perhaps connected with {{m|ga|ail||noble}}. Compare {{cog|fr|Alain}}.

brittany.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Bretany}}, {{m|enm|Brytany}}, itself borrowed from {{der|en|la-med|Britannia}}, applied to Brittany from at least the 6th century, and reinforced by {{der|en|frm|Bretagne}}. See {{m|la|Britannia}} for more. {{doublet|en|Britain|Britannia}}.

liam.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|ga|Liam}}, a clipping of {{m|ga|Uilliam}}, itself from {{der|en|en|William}}.

irene.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Irène}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εἰρήνη||peace}}, name of a goddess of peace, of early Christian saints, and of an 8th-century [[Byzantine]] [[empress]]. {{doublet|en|Eirini}}.

wayne.etyRaw: An occupational surname for a [[cartwright]], {{der|en|ang|wægen||wagon}}. Cf. {{m|en|wain}}.

ella.etyRaw: A 19th-century shortening of {{m|en|Eleanor}} or {{m|en|Ellen}}, later also used for any name ending in {{m|en||-ella}}, such as {{m|en|Gabriella}} or {{m|en|Daniella}}. Similar abbreviations have been formed independently in many European languages, for any name containing the syllable {{m|en||-el-}}, e.g. {{m|en|Elisabeth}}.

bonnie.etyRaw: Originally an American nickname from Scottish {{m|en|bonnie||fine, beautiful}}.

josephine.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Joséphine}}, diminutive of {{m|fr|Josèphe}}, feminine form of {{m|fr|Joseph}}. {{surf|en|Joseph|-ine<id:female>}}. Popularized in English by {{w|Josephine Bonaparte}}, the empress of {{w|Napoleonic France}}.

isaac.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Ysaac}}, from {{der|en|la|Isaac}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰσαάκ}}, from {{der|en|he|יצחק|lit=he laughs, he will laugh|tr=Yiṣḥāq}}. Explained in {{w|Book of Genesis|Genesis}} as referring to his mother [[Sarah]]’s laughing when she was told she would have a son at her old age. The verb is masculine, however, perhaps due to its use as a boy’s name.

victor.etyRaw: From a {{lbor|en|la-lat|-|notext=1}} personal name {{m|la|Victor}}, borne by several saints, from {{m|la|victor||conqueror}}. {{dbt|en|victor}}.

lucas.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Lucas}}, from {{der|en|grc|Λουκᾶς}}. See the Greek entry for more.

erin.etyRaw: Anglicisation of {{bor|en|ga|Éirinn|pos=dative singular and dialectal nominative singular of {{m|ga|Éire||Ireland}}}}.

anne.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Anne||[[Ann]]}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[Vulgate]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα}} in the [[New Testament]], from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. Occasionally reborrowed from languages who adopted the name from English. Very infrequently from {{bor|en|et|-}} abbreviation of {{m|et|Anna}} instead. {{doublet|en|Ann|Ana|Anna|Hannah}}. Compare {{m|en|John}}.

caleb.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la-lat|Caleb}}, {{m|la|Calebus}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Χάλεβ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|כָּלֵב||tr=Kālēḇ}}, possibly related to  {{m|hbo|כֶּלֶב||tr=keleḇ|dog}}, referring to the unconditional devotion of dogs to their masters.

luke.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Lūcās}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Λουκᾶς}}. See the Greek entry for more.

allison.etyRaw: From a {{inh|en|enm|-}} diminutive form of {{m|en|Alan}}, {{m|en|Alexander}} or {{af|en|Alice|-son}}.

phyllis.etyRaw: From the masculine {{bor|en|grc|Φύλλις}} or from the feminine {{m|grc|Φυλλίς}}.

johnny.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|John|y}}. In the sense of an Englishman, compare {{m|en|John Bull}}.

alyssa.etyRaw: A 20th-century invention. Possible origins: * From {{suffix|en|alyssum<alt:alyss(um)><t:a plant of the genus {{taxfmt|Alyssum|genus}}>|a}}. * From {{m|en|Alicia}}, of {{der|en|gem}} origin. * From {{m|en|Elissa}}.

tracy.etyRaw: A Norman baronial surname from places in France, derived from the Gallo-Roman given name ''[[Thracius]]'' which referred to ''[[Thrace]]'' + the Celtic suffix ''*-āko'' (place, property). As a female given name, it is also known as a diminutive of ''[[Theresa]]''.

martin.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Martin}}, from {{der|en|la|Mārtīnus|t=of or like Mars” or “little Mars}}, {{af|la|Mars|alt1=Mārs, Mārtis|-īnus|pos2=diminutive suffix|nocat=1}}. See {{m|la|Mārs}} for further etymology.

travis.etyRaw: From an {{der|en|fro|-}} word meaning "to cross over," related to {{m|en|traverse}}. Probably a name for a gatekeeper or the toll collector of a bridge. {{etystub|en|Please specify the Old French root if it is known.}}

ernest.etyRaw: Borrowed in the 18th century from {{m|de|Ernst}}, a medieval royal name in Germany, from {{der|en|goh|ernust|t=vigor, strife}}, only remotely related to modern {{cog|de|ernst}} or {{cog|en|earnest}}.

stanley.etyRaw: From places in England, {{der|en|ang|stān||stone}} + {{m|ang|lēah||meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|stone|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}. * The given name has also been used as an anglicisation of [[Stanisław]], [[Stanislav]] and related names. The coastal town in Hong Kong is {{named-after|en|Edward Henry Stanley, 15th Earl of Derby|wplink==|nocap=1}}.

clara.etyRaw: {{lbor|en|la|clāra}}, feminine of {{m|la|clārus|t=bright, shining, clear}}, a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara ([[Clare]]) of Assisi. {{dbt|en|Clare|Claire}}.

edna.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|עֶדְנָה|t=[[pleasure]]; [[delight]]}}; a variant of [[Eden]] in the Book of Tobit. In [[Ireland]] and [[Scotland]] it has been used as an anglicization of {{m|ga|Eithne}}.

alex.etyRaw: {{clipping|en|Alexander}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος}} 'he who wards off men', i.e. protector, possibly of Hittite origin. Also from {{m|en|Alexius}}, from the same Ancient Greek first element, "helping, defending". These two origins of Alex are [[indistinguishable]] in most languages. The female name has the same root, a {{clipping|en|Alexandra|nocap=1}} or the female name {{m|en|Alexis}}, in some cases also a spelling variant of {{m|en|Alix}}.

leonard.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Leonard}}, name of a 6th century Frankish saint, from {{der|en|goh|leo||lion}} or {{der|en|goh|liut||person}}  and {{m|goh|hart||hard}}. As a surname, also used as an anglicisation of {{bor|en|ga|Ó Leannáin}} ([[Lennon]]).

lee.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|lēa}}, the dative case of {{m|ang|lēah||meadow}}, originally to denote someone who lived near a meadow.

evan.etyRaw: Anglicization of {{bor|en|cy|Ifan}}, ultimately from {{der|en|la|Jōhannēs}}, variant of {{m|la|Iōannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=yōḥānān, yokhanán|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}. {{doublet|en|Giovanni|Ian|Ivan|Jack|Jean|Johan|Johann|Johannes|John|Sean|Shane|Shaun|Shawn}}.

tina.etyRaw: Short form of {{l|en|Christina}} or of any female name ending in ''-tina'', such as {{l|en|Martina}} or {{l|en|Albertina}}; frequently from {{der|en|la|-ina}}

nathaniel.etyRaw: Modification, under influence of {{m|en|Daniel}}, of {{m|en|Nathanael}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ναθαναήλ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|נְתַנְאֵל|tr=Netan'el|lit=God has given}}.<ref>Hanks, Patrick, et al. ''Oxford Dictionary of First Names (Second Edition)''. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006. Print.</ref>

adrian.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Hadrianus||from the Roman harbor Hadria}} a place name ultimately from {{der|en|ett|𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀}}. {{doublet|en|Hadrian}}. See {{w|Adria}}.

clarence.etyRaw: Originally a ducal title of the English and British royal family, from {{m|la|Clārensis|t=from the town of Clare}}, (the town of Clare, Suffolk), although it has also been associated with {{der|en|it|Chiarenza}}, {{m|it|Clarentza}}, &c., a former fortress and settlement in the medieval [[Frankish]] [[principality|Principality]] of [[Achaea]] in [[Greece]].

rita.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|roa|Rita}} {{gloss|{{bor|en|it|Rita}}, {{bor|en|es|Rita}}}}. A shortening of {{der|en|it|Margherita}}, and {{der|en|es|Margarita}}, cognates of English {{m|en|Margaret}}. An Italian {{w|Rita of Cascia|Saint Rita}} was [[canonize]]d in 1900. The English name came into regular use in early twentieth century.

eva.etyRaw: The ([[Vulgate]]) {{der|en|la|Eva}}, from {{der|en|grc|Εὔα|}}, from {{der|en|hbo|-}} {{m|he|חַוָּה|tr=ḥawwā}}. A Latinate variant of the English [[Eve]].

wanda.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|pl|Wanda}}, possibly derived from an ethnic term for “a [[Wend]]”.

joel.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|יוֹאֵל|tr=yo'él|t=[[Yahweh]] (is) God}}. As a medieval French and English given name, it is also from {{bor|en|br|Judicaël}} (related to {{m|en|Joyce}} and {{m|en|Jocelyn}}). Cf. {{m|en|Elijah}}.

courtney.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Courtenay}}, an aristocratic Norman surname derived from place names in Normandy, from {{der|en|la|Curtenus}}, a personal name from {{m|la|curtus||short}}.

amelia.etyRaw: A variant of [[Amalia]], derived from {{der|en|gem}} compound names beginning with {{m|gem-pro|*amal|t=vigor, bravery}}. For the first element, compare {{m|gem-pro|*ammōną|t=to bother, irritate}}. The name and its variants have been confused with the Latin name {{m|la|Aemilia}} (whence {{m|en|Emilia}}, {{m|en|Emily}}) and the French {{m|fr|Aimée}} (whence {{m|en|Amy}}).

ethel.etyRaw: Short form of names of {{der|en|ang|-}} origin beginning with Ethel-, {{m|ang|æþele||noble}}. First used in the 19th century. Cognate to the Germanic [[Adela]] and [[Adele]].

jayden.etyRaw: Invented at the end of the 20th century by American parents who wanted to combine the initial "J" with the fashionable sound of [[Aidan]], [[Braden]], [[Caden]] and [[Hayden]]. It has been [[unisex]] from the very beginning because it resembles both [[Jay]] and [[Jade]].

ellen.etyRaw: Medieval English variant of {{m|en|Helen}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἑλένη}}; also used as a variant of {{m|en|Eleanor}} or a feminine counterpart to {{m|en|Elliot}}.

marjorie.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Margery}}, a medieval vernacular form of {{m|en|Margaret}}.

esther.etyRaw: From {{der|en|grc|Ἐσθήρ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|אֶסְתֵּר|tr=ʾestēr}}. Has been connected to {{der|en|peo|𐎠𐎿𐎫𐎼|ts=star-|t=star}} (whence {{cog|pal|𐭮𐭲𐭫|ts=star|t=star}}, {{m|pal|𐭮𐭲𐭠𐭫𐭪|ts=stārag|t=star}}, {{cog|fa|ستاره||star|tr={{fa-xlit|سِتَارَه}}}}), from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂stḗr}} (if so, a distant {{doublet|en|star|nocap=1}}); or else to {{cog|akk|Ištar|𒀭𒈹|tr=Ištar|t=[[Ishtar]]}} ({{cog|he|עִשְׁתָּר||tr=ʿištār}}).

edith.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|ang|Ēadġȳþ}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*audaz||wealth, riches}} + {{m|gem-pro|*gunþiz||battle}}. Name of a 10th century English saint. Compare {{cog|sv|Edit}}.

morgan.etyRaw: from Old Welsh Morcant, possibly from {{m|cel-bry-pro|*mor||sea}} ({{cog|cy|môr}}) or {{m|cel-bry-pro|*mọr||great}} ({{cog|owl|maur}}) + {{m|cel-pro|*kantos||circle}} ({{cog|cy|cant}}), meaning “great chief” or “sea chief”.

oliver.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Oliver}}, from {{der|en|fro|Olivier}}, by folk etymology derived from the {{der|en|la|-}} name {{m|la|Olīvārius}}, but probably representing an {{der|en|goh|-}} form of {{der|en|non|Óleifr||ancestral + relic}} (modern {{cog|da|Olaf}} and {{cog|sv|Olof}}), or {{der|en|gem-pro|*ala-||all}} + {{m|gem-pro|*wēraz||true}} (modern {{cog|sv|allvar}}). Name of a [[paladin]] of [[Charlemagne]] in medieval French romance.

gladys.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{bor|en|cy|Gwladus}}, of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with {{m|cy|gwlad||country}}.

norma.etyRaw: Coined name of an imaginary [[Celtic]] priestess in Bellini's opera [[w:Norma (opera)|Norma]] (1831). Sometimes explained as {{uder|en|la|norma||pattern, model}}, or as a feminine form of {{m|en|Norman}}.

frederick.etyRaw: From {{der|en|de|Friedrich}}, {{m|de|Friederich}} and influenced by {{der|en|la|Friderīcus}}, {{m|la|Frederīcus}}, from {{der|en|goh|Fridurih}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Friþurīk}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Friþurīks}}, from {{compound|gem-pro|*friþuz<t:peace>|*rīks<t:king, ruler>|lit=peace king, peaceful ruler|nocat=1}}.

elaine.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Elaine}}, a variant of {{m|fro|Elene}}, cognate to {{m|en|Helen}}, ultimately from {{der|en|grc|Ἑλένη}}. A {{cog|cel}} origin has also been suggested since the name appears in [[Arthurian]] legend. {{doublet|en|Helen}}.

wendy.etyRaw: Popularized by the character in {{w|J. M. Barrie}}'s play, ''{{w|Peter and Wendy|Peter Pan}}'' (1904), though occasionally found earlier; the author explained that he got it from ''Fwendy-Wendy'' ("{{m|en|friend}}"), a nickname given to him by a child. Alternatively, from a diminutive of the {{cog|cy|Gwendolen}}; or from {{m|en|Wendelin}}, a diminutive of {{m|en|Wendel}}; therefore a {{doublet|en|Gwen|nocap=1}}. A habitational forename meaning, "island at the river bend", from {{inh|en|ang|wende||watercourse with a bend}} + {{m|ang|ēġ||island}}.

melanie.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Mélanie}}, from {{der|en|la|Melania}}, the name of two Roman fifth century saints, from {{der|en|grc|μέλας||black, dark}}.

marion.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Marion}}, from {{der|en|fro|Marion}}, a diminutive of [[Marie]], used in England since the Middle Ages.

leo.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|leō||lion}}, {{calque|la|grc|λέων|nocap=1|nocat=1}}, {{calque|grc|akk|𒉈𒍑|||tr=nēšu|nocap=1|nocat=1}}/{{calque|grc|akk|𒌨𒄞𒆷|||tr=urgulû|nocap=1|nocat=1|notext=1}}, from {{der|en|sux|𒌨𒄞𒆷||lion; name of constellation|tr=UR.GU.LA}}.<ref>John H. Roger "Origins of the ancient constellations: I. The Mesopotamian traditions" ''Journal of the British Astronomy Association'' '''108''': 1, p. 17.</ref> {{doublet|en|Leon|leu|lev|lion|Lyon}}.

jasmine.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|jasmin}}, from {{der|en|ar|يَاسَمِين}}, from {{der|en|fa-cls|یاسمین|tr=yāsamīn}}, from earlier {{m|fa-cls|یاسمن|tr=yāsaman}}, from {{der|en|pal|yʾsmn'|tr=yāsaman|sc=Latn}}.

cindy.etyRaw: Shortened from {{m|en|Lucinda}} and {{m|en|Cinderella}}. In the 20th century adopted as a pet form of {{m|en|Cynthia}}.

norman.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Norman}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Norman}} (a variant of {{m|ang|Norþman}}) and {{der|en|fro|Normant}}. It is certain that the word is derived from the base of the {{der|en|gem}} words for {{m|en|north}} and the Germanic base of the words for {{m|en|man}}. However, given the frequent movement of Germanic groups especially into and out of Britain in the post-classical world, it is unclear in what tongue it came to be used first. In addition, the generally accepted meaning, a person from Normandy or one of the many French-speaking invaders to Britain, was used chiefly by [[Anglo-Norman]] and {{der|en|fro|-}}, though it originally referred to any Scandinavian of the time. See also {{m|en|Northman}}.

chloe.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|grc|χλόη||young green shoot}}, an epithet of goddess [[Demeter]].

tony.etyRaw: {{clipping|en|Anthony//Antony}}. The statuettes awarded by the {{w|American Theatre Wing}} are formally known as “Antoinette Perry Awards for Excellence in Theatre”; they are named for {{w|Antoinette Perry}} (1888–1946), an actress, director, producer and co-founder of the American Theatre Wing, who was nicknamed Tony.

monica.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Mŏnĭca}}, name of the mother of [[w:Augustine of Hippo|St. Augustine]], of uncertain meaning but probably {{der|en|ber}} or {{der|en|phn|-}} origin.

wesley.etyRaw: Several places in England, from {{inh|en|ang|west||west}} + {{m|ang|lēah||wood, clearing}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|west|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.

edwin.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|ang|Ēadwine}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Audawini}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*Audawiniz}}. Akin to {{cog|non|Auðun}}, {{cog|is|Auðunn}}, {{cog|de|Otwin}}, {{cog|no|Audun}}, and the Lombard king's name [[w:Audoin|Audoin]] ({{cog|fr|Ouen}}).

rodney.etyRaw: From Old English placename {{m|ang||Hrōdanīeġ, Hrōdanīġ|lit=Hroda's island}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*hrōþiz||fame}} and {{m|gem-pro|*awjō||island}}.

riley.etyRaw: * From {{l|en|Ryley}} in [[Lancashire]], from {{der|en|ang|ryge||rye}} + {{m|ang|leah||clearing, meadow}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|rye|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}. * A variant of {{m|en|Reilly}}, from {{der|en|ga|Ó Raghallaigh}} (see {{m|en|O'Reilly}}).

jesus.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Jhesus}}, {{m|enm|Iesus}}, from {{der|en|la|Iēsūs}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰησοῦς}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יֵשׁוּעַ|tr=yēšū́aʿ}}, a contracted form of {{m|he|יְהוֹשֻׁעַ|tr=yəhōšúaʿ|gloss=[[Joshua]]}}, meaning "the Lord saves". The form {{m|he|יֵשׁוּעַ|tr=yēšū́aʿ}} is attested in some of the later books of the Hebrew Bible ([[w:Ezra–Nehemiah|Ezra–Nehemiah]]), and translated as [[Jeshua]] or [[Yeshua]] in some English editions (the former appearing in the [[King James Version]]). The Greek texts make no distinction between Jesus and [[Joshua]], referring to them both as {{m|grc|Ἰησοῦς}}. In the Wycliffe Bible (Middle English), the forms used are {{m|enm|Jhesus}} and {{m|enm|Jhesu}}.

dana.etyRaw: Of {{unc|en|nocap=1}} origin. Possibly from {{m|en|Dawnay}}, or else an altered form of {{m|en|Dan}} or {{m|en|Daniel}}.<ref>{{cite-book |last=Hanks |first=Patrick |title=[https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780190245115.001.0001/acref-9780190245115 Dictionary of American Family Names] |year=2022 |publisher={{w|Oxford University Press}} |isbn=9780190245115 |edition=second}}</ref>

alexandra.etyRaw: From {{der|en|grc|Ἀλεξάνδρα}}, from {{af|grc|ἀλέξω|t1=to defend|ἀνδρός|alt2=ἀνδρ-|pos2=stem of {{m|grc|ἀνήρ|t=man}}|nocat=1}}. Feminine form of ''[[Alexander]] ''(“the man who repels [enemies]”). The community in Prince Edward Island is named after {{w|Queen Alexandra}} (1844–1925).

sylvia.etyRaw: Feminine form of a Medieval form of [[Silvius]], from {{uder|en|la|silva||forest}}. In myths, Rhea Silvia was the mother of famous twins [[Romulus]] and [[Remus]], the founders of [[Rome]]. 6th-century saint Silvia was the mother of the [[pope]] Gregory the Great.

alfred.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Alfred}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ælfrǣd}}, from {{af|ang|ælf|t1=elf|rǣd|t2=counsel|nocat=1}}. {{doublet|en|Alfredo|Avery}}. Equivalent to [[elf]] + [[rede]]. The modern pronunciation with {{IPAchar|/f/}} is a spelling pronunciation; the name in Old English was pronounced with {{IPAchar|[v]}}, as shown in its Middle English descendant ''Alured'' (in which ''u'' stands for modern ''v'').

april.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|apprile}}, {{m|en|Aprill}}, re-Latinised from {{cog|enm|aueril}}, from {{der|en|fro|avrill}}, from {{der|en|la|Aprīlis||of the month of the goddess [[Venus]]}}, perhaps based on {{der|en|ett|𐌀𐌐𐌓𐌖}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀφροδίτη||Venus}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|ēastermōnaþ|t=April|lit=Easter month}}, see {{m|en|Eastermonth}}.

melvin.etyRaw: Variant of the Scottish surname [[Melville]], from a place name [[Malleville]] in Normandy, from {{der|en|la|mala||bad}} + {{der|en|fro|ville||settlement}}. * Used to Anglicize {{m|gd|Mac Gille Beathain}} in Scotland and {{m|ga|Ó Maoil Mhín}} in Ireland.

steve.etyRaw: Shortening of various names ultimately derived from {{der|en|la|Stephanus|g=m}}, from {{der|en|grc|Στέφανος|g=m}} from {{m|grc|στέφανος|g=m|t=crown, wreath}}

derek.etyRaw: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from a {{der|en|gml|-}} variant of [[Theodoric]], and revived in the 19th century.<ref>{{cite-book|en|2001|w:Patrick Hanks|author2=Flavia Hodges|A Concise Dictionary of First Names|publisher=w:Oxford University Press|edition=3rd|isbn=9780198662594}}</ref>

avery.etyRaw: From {{der|en|xno|Averay}}, {{m|fro|xno|Auveray}}, {{m|fro|xno|Alverey}}, from {{der|en|la|Alveredus}}, {{m|fro|xno|Aluredus}}, from {{der|en|ang|Ælfræd}}, from {{m|ang|ælf|t=elf}} and {{m|ang|ræd|t=counsel}}. {{doublet|en|Alfred}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hanks |first=Patrick |url=http://archive.org/details/dictionaryoffirs0000hank_l4f5 |title=A Dictionary of First Names |year=2006 |publisher=Oxford ; New York : Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-861060-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |en|last=Redmonds |first=George |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9LzJ5OnKMKsC&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&lpg=PP1&pg=PA67#v=onepage&q&f=false |title=Christian Names in Local and Family History |date=2004-04-13 |publisher=Dundurn |isbn=978-1-55488-132-1 }}</ref>

lucy.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Lucy}}, from {{der|en|fro|Lucie}} (notably after the Christian martyr {{w|Saint Lucy|Lucia of Syracuse}}), from {{der|en|la|Lucia}} (feminine of {{m|la|Lucius}}, a Roman [[praenomen]]), from {{m|la|lux||light}}. The name of the {{taxfmt|Australopithecus|genus}} skeleton came from the [[Beatles]] song “{{w|Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds}}”, which was being played repeatedly at the dig site camp at the time of the discovery. The slang term for LSD also derives from the song name, which many believe is essentially a reference to the drug.<ref>{{R:Greens|id=ihjkiki|head=lucy in the sky with diamonds|pos=n}}</ref>

vanessa.etyRaw: {{coin|en|Jonathan Swift|in=the 18th century|nobycat=1}} as a pseudonym for a lady friend named {{w|Esther Vanhomrigh}} (or Van Homrigh), an Irish woman of Dutch descent, by taking the {{der|en|nl|-}} preposition {{m|nl|van}} from her surname and adding ''-essa'' (perhaps influenced by the first syllable of {{m|en|Esther}}).<ref>Paul J. DeGategno, R. Jay Stubblefield, ''Critical Companion to Jonathan Swift'' (2006), page 42</ref><ref>{{R:en:DFN|page=269|column=2}}</ref>

connor.etyRaw: The first name is from {{der|en|ga|Conchúr}}, {{m|ga|Conchobhar}}, from {{der|en|sga|Conchobar||lover of hounds}}. The surname is from {{der|en|ga|Ó Conchúir||descendant of Conchúr}}.

erica.etyRaw: A feminine form of {{m|en|Eric}}, ultimately from {{der|en|non|-}}. The name has also been associated with the flower genus.

alicia.etyRaw: A [[Latinization]] of {{m|en|Alice}}, which is in turn from {{der|en|fro|Adelais}}, {{der|en|gem|-}} {{m|goh|Adalheid}}.

vivian.etyRaw: Early saints' name from {{bor|en|la|Vīviānus}}, and of its feminine form {{m|la|Vīviāna}}, probably from {{m|la|vīvus|t=alive}}.

pauline.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Pauline}}, in turn from {{der|en|la|Paulīna}}; in regular use since the 19th century. {{surf|en|Paul|-ine<pos:feminine suffix>}}.

chad.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Chadde}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ċeadda}}, of obscure meaning; name of a seventh-century [[Anglo-Saxon]] saint, revived in the 20th century. The sense of “alpha male” originates from an apparent stereotype that men with such a name tend to bear that temperament, {{etydate|c|late 1990s in {{w|Chicago, Illinois}} (specifically "successful white man, [[yuppie]]")|late 2010s via {{w|4chan}} and {{w|California}} slang|nocap=1}}.

kristen.etyRaw: A spelling variant of {{m|en|Kristin}}, from {{m|en|Christina}}, fairly popular in the latter half of the twentieth century.

sebastian.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Sebastiānus}}, name of an early [[Christian]] saint, from ancient city of {{w|Sebaste}} in [[Asia Minor]] (modern {{w|Sivas}}, Turkey), from {{der|en|grc|Σεβαστός||august, venerable, exalted}}, itself a translation of the Roman title {{m|la|Augustus}}.

carter.etyRaw: As an English name, from the occupation {{m|en|carter}}. As an Irish name, from {{der|en|ga|Mac Artúir|lit=son of Arthur}}.

kim.etyRaw: {{clipping|en|Kimball}} and {{m|en|Kimberley}} as a male name, and of {{m|en|Kimberley}} and {{m|en|Kimberly}} as a female name.

oscar.etyRaw: Exact origin {{unc|en|nocap=1}}. Resuscitated by James Mcpherson in ''The Works of Ossian'' (1765). [[Napoleon]], an admirer of the Ossianic poems, chose it for his godson {{w|Oscar I of Sweden|Oscar Bernadotte}}, who became a king of Sweden. The modern given name is a conflation of two unrelated names: first, {{bor|en|mga|Oscar|pos=the name of Fionn Mac Cumhaill's grandson in Irish mythology}}, from {{der|en|mga|-}} {{m|ga|os|t=deer}} + {{m|mga|cara|t=friend}}; and second, {{inh|en|ang|Ōscār}}, {{m|ang|Ōsgār|lit=spear of the gods/spear of God|pos=personal name}}, from {{der|en|ang|ōs|t=god}} and {{m|ang|gār|t=spear}} (see [[Oswald]]). Compare {{cog|de|Ansgar|pos=personal name}}, {{cog|da|Asker}}, {{m|da|Asger|pos=personal name}}, {{cog|no|Asgeir|pos=personal name}}, {{cog|is|Ásgeir|pos=personal name}}. {{sense|Academy Award}} Disputed. Said to have been named by actress Bette Davis after her first husband, Harmon Oscar Nelson, or by secretary Margaret Herrick after her cousin Oscar Pierce.

claire.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Claire}}, also a spelling variant of the {{cog|en|Clare}}.

joanne.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Joanne}}, from {{der|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

geraldine.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Gerald|ine}}. c. 1540 by the Earl of Surrey as a poetic name for Lady Elizabeth Fitzgerald, "one of the Fitzgeralds". Taken up as a given name in the 19th century, and used as a feminine form of [[Gerald]].

ray.etyRaw: * As an English surname, from pet forms derived from the root of {{m|en|Raymond}}. * Also as an English surname, from {{der|en|fro|rei|t=king}}. Compare {{m|en|Roy}}, {{m|en|King}}. * Also as an English surname, from {{der|en|ang|rā|t=[[roe]] deer}}. Compare {{m|en|Roe}}. * Also as an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Wray}} and {{m|en|Rye}}. * As a {{der|en|gd|-}} surname, shortened from {{m|en|McRae}}. * As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, from the verb {{m|fr|raier|t=to gush out, flow, radiate}}. Compare {{m|en|Leray}}. * As a {{der|en|pl|-}} and {{der|en|sl|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Raj}}, from {{m|pl|raj|t=paradise}}. * As an Indian surname, variant of {{m|en|Rai}}.

wyatt.etyRaw: Ultimately from the {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|Wigheard}}, from {{m|ang|wīg||war}} + {{m|ang|heard||hard, brave}}, later also used as a {{der|en|enm|-}} diminutive of the names {{m|en|Guy}} and {{m|en|William}}.

bertha.etyRaw: Definitely from {{der|en|ang|Berþa}} as a result of metathesis of h, from earlier {{der|en|ang|Berhte||bright one}}, influence of Latin [[Bercta]]. Alternatively, from {{der|en|goh|berhta||bright one}}, which was an [[epithet]] of the goddess [[Frigg]].

june.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|June}}, {{m|enm|june}}, re-Latinised variants of earlier {{der|en|enm|Juyn}}, {{m|enm|juyng}}, from {{der|en|fro|juing}}, {{m|fro|juin}}, from {{der|en|la|iūnius}}, the month of the goddess {{m|la|Iuno||Juno}}, perhaps from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂yéwHō}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂óyu||vital force, youthful vigor}}.

juanita.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|es|Juanita}}, from {{m|es|Juana}} + {{m|es|-ita||[[-ette]]}}, from {{der|en|osp|Johanna}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Janet|Jeanette|Jeannette|Shanae|Sinead}}.

jill.etyRaw: A variant of {{m|en|Gill}}, diminutive of {{m|en|Gillian}}, a medieval form of {{m|en|Juliana}}, ultimately from {{uder|en|la|-}}.

stella.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|stēlla||star}}. {{senseno|en|black woman who visits Jamaica as a sex tourist|cap=1}} is after the protagonist of ''{{w|How Stella Got Her Groove Back}}'' (1998).

jared.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Iared}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰαρέδ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|יֶרֶד|tr=yéred}}. Often explained as deriving from the root {{m|he|י־ר־ד|tr=y-r-d}}, which forms words relating to descending (see [[Jordan]] and [[ירדן]] for more); some interpret the [[w:Book of Enoch|Book of Enoch]] as suggesting that the Jared in the Bible was so named because it was in his time that two hundred angels descended from Heaven to Mount Hermon. Alternatively, sometimes explained as deriving from the root {{m|he|ר־ד־ה|tr=r-d-}}, which forms words relating to ruling.

blake.etyRaw: A surname derived from either {{der|en|ang|blæc||black}} or from {{der|en|ang|blāc||pale, fair, shining, white}}, or as an anglicisation of {{der|en|ga|Ó Bláthmaic}}.

holly.etyRaw: {{swp|<dab!>}} * As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, calque of {{m|ga|mac}} {{m|ga|cuilinn|t=holly}} (see {{m|en|McCullen}}) and sometimes {{m|en|McQuillan}}. * As an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Holley}}. * As a {{der|en|cs|-}} and {{der|en|sk|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Holý}}, {{m|en|Holy}}. * Also as a locational English surname, from {{der|en|ang|hol}} {{m|ang|leah|t=wood, clearing, meadow}}, compare {{m|en|Hollywood}}. * Also as an English surname, short form of {{m|en|Holiday}}. * Also as an English surname, after the {{m|en|holly}} tree. * As a feminine given name popularized by Truman Capote's {{w|Breakfast at Tiffany's}} (especially the 1961 film adaptation starring Audrey Hepburn).

sally.etyRaw: A diminutive [[lambdacism]] of {{m|en|Sarah}}. Compare {{m|en|Hal}} from {{m|en|Harry}} and {{m|en|Moll}} from {{m|en|Mary}}.

darlene.etyRaw: A 20th-century coinage from {{m|en|darling}} and names like {{m|en|Charlene}} and {{m|en|Marlene}}.

brooke.etyRaw: A [[topographic]] surname for someone who lived near a [[brook]].

bernard.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Bernard}}, from {{der|en|fro|Bernard}}, {{m|fro|Bernart}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Bernardus}}, probably from {{der|en|frk|*Bernhard}} (cognate with {{cog|goh|Bernhart}}, {{cog|ang|Beornheard}}), from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Bernuharduz}}, equivalent to {{af|en|bear|-ard|nocat=1}}. Popularized by medieval European saints.

randall.etyRaw: A {{inh|en|enm|-}} variant of [[Randolph]], preserved as a surname and revived in the twentieth century.

lorraine.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Loreyne}}, from {{der|en|fro|Loherraine}}, from {{m|fro|loherenc|t=Lotharingian}}; compare {{cog|la-eme|Lotharingia}} (ultimately named for {{w|Lothair II}}, who ruled it); compare {{doublet|en|Lotharingia|notext=1}}, {{cog|de|Lothringen}}.

shane.etyRaw: Anglicized form of the Northern Irish pronunciation of {{bor|en|ga|Seán}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehan}}, from {{der|en|la|Johannes}}, variant of {{m|la|Ioannes}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}. {{doublet|en|John|Jack|Johan|Johann|Johannes|Jean|Ian|Evan|Ivan|Sean|Shaun|Giovanni}} as a male name. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}} as a female name.

dean.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|la-med|gkm}} The surname or given name is of multiple origins, depending on context: * As an English surname, from {{der|en|enm|dene|t=valley}}. * Also as an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|dean}}. Cognate to {{m|en|Deacon}}. * Also as an English surname, from the personal name {{m|en|Deyne}}, a rhyming form of {{m|en|Reynald}} (see {{m|en|Reginald}}). * As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Deane}}. * As a Scottish surname, from {{w|Dean Castle}} in [[Kilmarnock]], itself from the noun meaning valley. * {{inh|en|ang|Dene||Dane, Norseman}} * {{der|en|he|דין||law, judgment}} and {{der|en|ar|دين||way of life, creed}}

beatrice.etyRaw: Either 1) from the {{der|en|la|Beatrix}}, name of early Christian saints, from {{m|la|beatrix||she who makes happy}}, or 2) from {{m|la|beata}}, influenced by {{m|la|viātrīx|viatrix}} (“female wayfarer, traveller”).

casey.etyRaw: Anglicisation of an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname {{m|ga|Ó Cathasaigh|lit=descendant of (a person named) Watchful}}.

leroy.etyRaw: Transferred from the common {{der|en|fr|-}} surname {{m|fr|Leroy}}, meaning "the king".

nora.etyRaw: Short form of {{m|en|Eleanor}} or, rarely, of {{m|en|Honora}}.

savannah.etyRaw: The cities are named after the {{m|en|Savannah River}}, possibly derived from {{uder|en|sjw|-}} or {{uder|en|alg|-}}.

clifford.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|clif||cliff}} + {{m|ang|ford||ford}}, ''a dweller at the ford by the steep bank''.

elsie.etyRaw: From a Scottish diminutive of [[Alison]]/[[Alice]] and [[Elspeth]]/[[Elizabeth]].

gavin.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|cel|cel-bry|cel-bry-pro|cel-pro}} Medieval variant of {{m|en|Gawain}}, the name of an [[Arthurian]] knight, first recorded as {{m+|fro|Gauvain}}. The form ''Gavin'' survived in Scotland and spread to other English-speaking countries in the 1960s. {{doublet|en|Gawain}}.<ref>Bolton, Lesley (2009). The Complete Book of Baby Names. Sourcebooks, Inc</ref>

lily.etyRaw: A 19th-century flower name, from {{m|en|lily}}. Also a [[diminutive]] of {{m|en|Lilian}} and sometimes {{m|en|Elizabeth}}.

ida.etyRaw: Short form of obsolete names beginning with Germanic ''īd'' "work", used for both sexes in medieval England. It was revived in the 19th century, partly mistaken for a Greek name, for the Mount Ida of classical mythology.

sydney.etyRaw: For the surname and given name, see {{m|en|Sidney}}. The cities in Australia and Canada are named after British politician {{w|Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney}} (1733–1800).

lydia.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|grc|Λυδία||the region of Lydia}}, from {{m|grc|λυδία||[[beautiful]] one, [[noble]] one}}, a [[feminine]] form of {{m|grc|Λυδός}} ([[Lydus]], from {{m|grc|λυδός}} ([[lydus]])).  The region of Lydia is said to be named for a king {{m|grc|Λυδός}} ([[Lydus]], from {{m|grc|λυδός}} ([[lydus]])); the given name Lydia originally indicated ancestry or residence in the region of Lydia.

eileen.etyRaw: From Anglicized forms of {{bor|en|ga|Eibhlín}}, {{m|ga|Eilín}} or {{m|ga|Aibhilín}} in {{inh|en|enm|-}} and Modern English, all cognates of {{doublet|en|Evelyn|notext=1}} from {{der|en|fro|Aveline}}. Sometimes also used for the Irish name {{m|ga|Éibhleann}}, possibly from {{der|en|sga|oíph||radiance, beauty}}.

sofia.etyRaw: Variant spelling of {{m|en|Sophia}} and from various other languages' own adaptations of {{der|en|grc|Σοφία||[[wisdom]], especially [[divine]] [[wisdom]]}}. Sometimes borrowed into English as an anglicization of an accented or closely related form, as with Spanish {{m|es|Sofía}}, Welsh {{m|cy|Soffia}}, and Hungarian {{m|hu|Zsófia}}.
