As the capital of Bulgaria, via nonstandard, though [[w:Romanization of Bulgarian#Streamlined System with -ia-exception|now official]], romanization of {{bor|en|bg|Со́фия}}, from {{m|bg|[[църква]] „[[света|Света]] [[София]]“}}, from {{der|en|gkm|[[ναός|Ναός]] [[ἁγία|Ἁγίας]] [[Σοφία|Σοφίας]]|t=[[church|Church]] of [[holy|Holy]] [[wisdom|Wisdom]]}}, the city's prominent {{w|Church of St. Sofia|6th-century Byzantine Greek church}}, first attested being used as the name for the city in the 14th century and reinforced under Ottoman rule as {{der|en|ota|صوفیه|tr=Sofya}}. Compare the name of the {{m|en|Hagia Sophia}}.

violet.etyRaw: A 19th century flower name from {{m|en|violet}}, sometimes as an anglicisation of the earlier {{uder|en|fr|Violette}}.

regina.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|la|rēgīna||queen}}. The given name originally referred to the [[Virgin Mary]] as the [[Queen of Heaven]]. The Canadian city was named for Queen Victoria, as suggested by Princess Louise. {{doublet|en|rani}}.

leon.etyRaw: Ultimately from {{bor|en|la|Leo}} and {{m|la|leo||[[lion]]}}, from {{der|en|grc|Λέων}} and {{m|grc|λέων||[[lion]]}}, likely ultimately from a non-Indo-European language. Sometimes via other related languages such as {{der|en|fr|Léon}} and sometimes as a diminutive of related names such as {{m|en|Leonard}} and {{m|en|Leonardo}}.

barry.etyRaw: Anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Bairre}}, short form of {{m|ga|Fionnbharr}}, from {{m|ga|fionn||white}} + {{m|ga|barr||head}}.

kristin.etyRaw: Borrowed in the 20th century from {{uder|en|no|Kristin}}, a variant of [[Christina]].

jo.etyRaw: [[clipping|Clipping]] or [[hypochoristic]] form of various female given names beginning with ''Jo...'', primarily {{m|en|Joan}}, {{m|en|Joanna}}, etc. but also {{m|en|Josephine}} and {{m|en|Jolene}}. {{dbt|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenna|Jenny|Jessie|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} in reference to the first derivation.

warren.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|xno|-}} surname {{m|xno|[[w:Warenne family|(de) Warenne]]}}, a reference to a place called [[Varenne]], a hamlet near {{w|Arques-la-Bataille}}, along the river {{w|Varenne (Arques)|Varenne}} in [[Normandy]], from {{der|en|la-med|Warinna}}, a hydronym of {{der|en|cel}}/{{der|en|cel-gau|-}} origin, from {{m|cel-gau|*var-}}, {{m|cel-gau|*ver-|t=river, water}}, ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂wer-||water, rain, flow}}; see also the Latin river {{m|la|Avara}}. Phonetic {{der|en|gem|-}} influence is shown by the [v] > [w].<ref>François de Beaurepaire, La Vintlana était-elle la Bresle ou la rivière de Cailly ?, Annales de Normandie, 1960, Vol. 10, Numbers 10-1, p. 63.</ref>

aubrey.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Aubrey}}, {{m|enm|Aubry}}, from {{der|en|nrf|Auberi}}, {{m|nrf|Alberi}}, from {{der|en|la|Alberīcus}}, Latinized form of {{der|en|goh|Alberich}}, from Proto-Germanic {{m|gem-pro|*Albirīks}}, from {{compound|gem-pro|*albiz|t1=elf, fairy|*rīks|t2=king, ruler|nocat=1}}. Possibly influenced by {{cog|cel-gau|Albiorix|Albiorīx}} (literally "ruler of the world"). Cognates include {{cog|de|Alberich}} and {{cog|it|Alberico}}.

jeanne.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Jeanne}}, from {{der|en|frm|Jehanne}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Johanna}}, variant of {{der|en|la|Ioanna}} under influence from {{der|en|la|Iōhannēs}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

rosemary.etyRaw: A combination of {{compound|en|Rose|Mary}}, referring to the flower as a symbol of [[Virgin Mary]], first recorded in the eighteenth century. It is found in continental Europe as [[Rosemarie]] and [[Rosa]] [[Maria]]. After mid-nineteenth century when flower names became common it may also refer to the herb [[rosemary]], Latin ''ros marinus'' "dew of the sea".

colleen.etyRaw: From the word {{m|en|colleen}}, from {{der|en|ga|cailín||girl}}, not used as a name in Ireland. Colleen can also be interpreted as a variant of [[Coleen]], which was a product of marketing by the Hollywood film industry (to promote a new starlet in the 1920s).

pearl.etyRaw: From {{m|en|pearl}}. * {{sense|river in China}} From {{der|en|zh|珠江||Pearl River|tr=Zhūjiāng, Zyu1 Gong1}}; {{calque|en|zh|珠||pearl|tr=zhū, zyu1|nocap=1}}. * {{sense|haven in Hawaii}} From {{der|en|haw|Wai Momi|t=pearl water}}; {{calque|en|haw|momi||pearl|nocap=1}}.

addison.etyRaw: A [[Appendix:Glossary#patronimic|patronymic]] surname from a medieval diminutive form of {{suffix|en|Adam|son}}.

jerome.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|fro|-}} vernacular form of the saint's name [[Hieronymus]], from {{der|en|grc|Ἱερώνυμος}}. {{doublet|en|Geronimo|Hieronymus}}.

xavier.etyRaw: Toponymic surname of a 16th-century saint born in the Kingdom of Navarre, Francis de Xavier, from a place name in the Kingdom of [[Navarre]], originally from {{der|en|eu|Xabier}}. Doublet of {{m|es|Echeverría}}.

bill.etyRaw: Hypocorism of {{m|en|William}}. It is unclear how the initial ''W'' became a ''B;'' this could have been part of the medieval trend of swapping letters, similar to {{m|en|Dick}} for {{m|en|Rick}}. <!--Through an intermediate V probably, as [w]/[v] mutations and [v]/[b] mutations are common in many languages. But where would be the trace of anyone named "Vill" in English? But note that there is "Vilhelm" in several Scandinavian languages. As well the German pronunciation of w is [v] and Willy is a German nickname for Wilhelm.}} -->

darrell.etyRaw: Derived from [[d'Airel]], name of a [[Norman]] family that came from a place called [[Airelle]] in [[Calvados]].

carmen.etyRaw: From {{der|en|es|Carmen}}, cognate with {{m+|en|Carmel}}. Made famous outside Spain by the [[opera]] ''Carmen'' (1875) by [[w:Georges Bizet|Georges Bizet]].

daisy.etyRaw: From the flower [[daisy]], one of the flower names dating from the 19th century. Also a [[nickname]] for [[Margaret]], since [[Marguerite]] and [[Margarita]] are identical with the French and Spanish word for "daisy".

erik.etyRaw: A spelling variant of {{m|en|Eric}}, or directly borrowed from modern {{bor|en|sv|Erik}}.

edgar.etyRaw: From {{der|en|ang|Ēadgār}}, the name of early English kings, from {{der|en|ang|ēad||rich}} + {{m|ang|gār||spear}}. Compare {{cog|is|Auðgeir}}. Hairstyle named after Major League Baseball player Edgar Martínez.

yvonne.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} feminine form of [[Yvon]], variant of [[Yves]], from a {{der|en|gem}} root for "[[yew]]" (see {{cog|ang|iw}}). It might have originally been used of an [[archer]], since yew wood was used to make bows.

micheal.etyRaw: Anglicised form of {{cog|ga|Mícheál}} or {{cog|gd|Mìcheal}}. Also a spelling variant of {{m|en|Michael}}, generally considered erroneous.

cora.etyRaw: Apparently brought up in English literature by James Fenimore Cooper in ''The Last of the Mohicans'' (1826), but compare a female heroine of this name in Jean-François Marmontel's ''Les Incas'' (1777) and the {{der|en|grc|-}} epithet {{m|grc|Κόρη}} for {{m|grc|Περσεφόνη}}. It could also refer directly to {{m|grc|κόρη||maiden}}.

floyd.etyRaw: Anglicisation of the Welsh name {{lang|cy|Lloyd}}, from {{der|en|cy|llwyd||[[grey]], grey-haired}}.

cole.etyRaw: The surname is variously from: # A nickname from {{der|en|ang|col||coal, coal-black}}, # A patronymic from {{m|en|Nicholas}} (see also {{m|en|Coles}}, {{m|en|Colson}}, {{m|en|Colle}}). # A variation of {{m|en|Cowell}} (which itself has several origins). # As an {{der|en|ga|-}} and {{der|en|gd|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|McCool}}. # As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Kohl}}. # As a {{der|en|nl|-}} surname, Americanized from {{m|en|Kool}}. # As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, Americanized/calqued from {{m|en|Charbonneau}}, influenced by the first sense.

gordon.etyRaw: The main etymology, associated with {{der|en|cel|-}} names, is from the {{bor|en|sco|-}} surname {{m|sco|Gordon}}, from a place name, but the origin is {{unc|en|debated}}: * If the English or Scots name is from a {{der|en|cel-bry|-}} language (such as {{der|en|owl|-}} or {{der|en|obt|-}}), then possibly from a {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|-}} compound such as {{com|cel-bry-pro|*gor|*din|t1=spacious|t2=fort|nocat=1}}; * If the Scots name is itself from English, then possibly from {{der|en|fr|Gourdon}}, derived from Gallo-Roman {{der|en|la|Gordus}}, from {{der|en|cel-gau||*Gordos}}; * Otherwise, possibly ultimately from {{uder|en|ang|*gordūn|*gor-dūn|mud hill}}{{attn|ang|attested??}} whence a habitational name. {{rfv-etym|en}}

gina.etyRaw: * {{sense|name from Greek}} {{clipping|en|Georgina}}. * {{sense|name from Latin}} {{clipping|en|Regina}}. * {{sense|name from Italian}} {{bor|en|it|Gina}}

nellie.etyRaw: Suffixed with {{af|en|-ie|id1=diminutive}}, compare {{m|en|Noll}} and {{m|en|Neddie}}, respectively from {{m|en|Oliver}} and {{m|en|Edward}}.

mario.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|it|-}} and {{bor|en|es|Mario}}, both of which coming from {{der|en|la|Marius}}.

ivan.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|ru|Ива́н}}, and from ''Ivan'' in several {{der|en|sla}} languages. {{doublet|en|John}} and its relatives {{doublet|en|Evan|Giovanni|Ian|Johann|Sean|notext=1}}, etc.

heidi.etyRaw: From Swiss {{der|en|de|Heidi}}, a pet form of {{m|de|Adelheid}}, equivalent of English [[Adelaide]] and [[Alice]]. The name became internationally popular due to the children's book ''{{w|Heidi}}'' (1880). {{C|en|Switzerland}} {{C|en|Fictional characters}}

jenna.etyRaw: A Cornish name, usually as a diminutive form of {{m|en|Jennifer}}. {{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenny|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} when based on {{m|en|Jenny}}'s other derivations.

vernon.etyRaw: From {{der|en|xtg||uerna|alder}} (from {{der|en|cel-pro|*wernā}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*wern-}}) + {{m|cel-gau||-o}}, {{m|cel-gau||-onis|pos=locative suffix|lit=place of alder trees}}.

paige.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Page}}, from {{m|en|[[page#Noun_2|page]]||}}, from {{der|en|fro|page}}, possibly via {{der|en|roa-oit|paggio}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|pagius||servant}}, probably from {{der|en|grc|παιδίον||boy, lad}}, from {{m|grc|παῖς||child}}; some sources consider this unlikely and suggest instead {{der|en|la|pagus||countryside}}, in sense of "boy from the rural regions".

hayden.etyRaw: Originally a place name, from {{inh|en|ang|heg||hay}} + {{m|ang|denu||valley}}. Alternatively, from {{der|en|dum|heiden||heathen}}.

alejandro.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|es|Alejandro}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἀλέξανδρος|lit=defender of man}}, an epithet of the goddess {{w|Hera Alexandros|Hera}}. {{doublet|en|Alexander}}.

lena.etyRaw: The female name is from the [[Scandinavian]], [[German]] and [[Russian]] pet form of [[Helena]], [[Magdalena]] and [[Yelena]] (also spelled [[Elena]]). The river in Yakutia is from {{bor|en|ru|Лена}}, from {{der|en|evn|Елюенэ||the Large River}}. Compare to {{cog|sah|Өлүөнэ}}. {{s|Norwegian river}} Probably related to Old Norse {{m|non|leir||clay}} (see the references). {{s|Town in Toten}} From {{der|en|non|lein}}.

maureen.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{bor|en|ga|Máirín}}, diminutive of {{m|ga|Máire}}, an Irish equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}}. {{surf|en|Maura|-een}}.

vera.etyRaw: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from the {{der|en|ru|-}} virtue name {{m|ru|Ве́ра||faith}}. By folk etymology it has also been explained as Latin {{m|la|vera||true}}.

joy.etyRaw: From the noun ''[[joy]]'', first used by [[Puritan]]s in the 17th century.

marian.etyRaw: A variant of [[Marion]], a medieval derivation of [[Mary]], often also interpreted as a [[contraction]] of [[Mary]] and [[Ann]], or as a variant of [[Mariana]].

clyde.etyRaw: From {{der|en|gd|Cluaidh}}, the name of a river in Scotland, of uncertain origin. Possibly influenced by ''clut'' (“the cleansing one”).

francisco.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Franciscus}}. {{doublet|en|Francis}}. * {{sense|given name}} From {{bor|en|roa}} ''Francisco'' ({{bor|en|pt|Francisco}}, {{bor|en|es|Francisco}}) * {{sense|moon of Uranus}} From the naming pattern established for moons of Uranus, being references to the works of {{w|lang=en|William Shakespeare}}. From being a character in the play {{w|lang=en|The Tempest}}

franklin.etyRaw: From {{der|en|enm|frankelein||freeholder}}, see {{m|en|franklin}}. The place names are mostly {{named-after|en|Benjamin Franklin|nat=American|occ=statesman|born=1706|died=1790|wplink==|nocap=1}}.

carson.etyRaw: Could originate from the Gaelic name "Carr" or "Carra", meaning "rock" or "fort," combined with "son", thus "son of Carr.".

arlene.etyRaw: A nineteenth-century coinage probably based on similar-sounding names such as [[Charlene]] and [[Arlette]].

kaylee.etyRaw: Coined toward the end of the 20th century * A combination of {{compound|en|Kay|Lee}}. * A variant of the surname {{m|en|Cayley}} or {{m|en|Keeley}}.

tom.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Thomme}}. {{U|hypocorism}} of {{m|en|Thomas}}. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of {{w|Thomas Jefferson}} featured on it.

brent.etyRaw: English surname from placenames in [[Devon]] and [[Somerset]], from {{der|en|ang|brant|t=steep}}, referring to hills. Compare {{m|en|Brents}}.

clayton.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Claytone}}, {{m|enm|Cleyton}}, from {{der|en|ang|clǣġ|t=clay}} + {{der|en|ang|tūn|t=enclosure, settlement; town}}. Analyzable as {{suffix|en|clay|ton}}.

gabrielle.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Gabrielle}}, feminine form of {{m|en|Gabriel}} (see there for more).

maurice.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Maurice}}, from {{der|en|la-lat|Mauritius}}, derived from {{m|la|Maurus||[[Moor]]; dark, swarthy}}. Popularized by a 3rd-century Roman soldier martyr.

myrtle.etyRaw: After the plant, {{m|en|myrtle}}; used since the end of the 19th century.

herman.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|here||army}} + {{m|ang|man||man}}<ref> Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges : A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001. </ref> It was revived in the 19th century, partly due to American immigrants from continental Europe where the name has been more popular. Compare the German equivalent {{m|de|Hermann}}.

grant.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|gd|Grannd}}, from {{der|en|xno|graunt|t=big, large}}, from {{der|en|fro|grant}}, from {{der|en|la|grandis}}. {{doublet|en|grand}}. The dollar-bill sense is from the portrait of {{w|Ulysses S. Grant}} featured on it.

garrett.etyRaw: A medieval English and Irish form of the {{der|en|gem}} [[given name]]s [[Gerard]] and [[Gerald]]. Of [[Old High German]] origin.

melinda.etyRaw: Coined in the eighteenth century from names such as {{m|en|Melanie}} and {{af|en|Melissa|-inda}}.

nolan.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{bor|en|ga|Ó Nualláin|lit=descendant of {{l|ga|Nuallán}}}}, diminutive of {{m|ga|nuall||chariot-fighter, champion}}.

lindsay.etyRaw: From [[Lindsey]] in [[Lincolnshire]], from {{inh|en|ang|Lindesēġe}}, {{m|ang|Lindesīġe|t=Isle of Lind}}, the Old English name of the city of [[Lincoln]], Lincolnshire, in which "Lind" comes from the Common Brittonic form of the name of Lincoln and "isle" refers to Lincoln being surrounded by fenland; from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*llɨnn||pool}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*lindos||lake, liquid}}, in reference to the [[w:Brayford Pool|Brayford]] + {{m+|ang|ēġ||island}}; cf. modern {{cog|cy|llyn}} and [[Dublin]].

colin.etyRaw: Diminutive of [[Coll]], a medieval short form of [[Nicholas]]. It has also been used to anglicize {{noncog|ga|Coileán}} and {{noncog|gd|Cailean}}.

charlene.etyRaw: A feminine form of {{m|en|Charles}} coined in the nineteenth century. Compare {{m|en|Marlene}}, {{m|en|Helene}} and {{m|en|Magdalene}} for the suffix.

nina.etyRaw: Borrowed into English in the nineteenth century, apparently from several sources. Many borrowings are of {{bor|en|ru|Ни́на}}, the name of a Georgian saint in the fourth century, also known as [[Nino]], of obscure origin and meaning, possibly connected with the [[Assyrian]] king [[Ninus]]. Others are of an {{bor|en|it|-}} short form of diminutives like {{m|it|Annina}} from {{m|it|Anna}} and {{m|it|Giovannina}} from {{m|it|Giovanna}}. Phonologically or orthographically similar names are present in several languages, including Afrikaans, Hindi, Italian, Persian, Romanian, Russian, Spanish and some Native American languages. In many of those, it is a nickname for names ending in ''-ina'' or ''-nina''. {{sense|hidden message in crossword}} After Nina Hirschfeld, the daughter of the American caricaturist {{w|Al Hirschfeld}}; her name was often concealed in his drawings.

isabel.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|es|Isabel}}, from {{der|en|pro|Elisabel}}, from {{der|en|la|Elisabeth}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ}}, from {{der|en|he|אֱלִישֶׁבַע|tr=Elishéva|t=my [[God]] is an oath}}. {{doublet|en|Elizabeth}}.

marcia.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Marcia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Marcius}}, a derivative of {{m|la|Marcus}}, ultimately from {{m|la|Mārs}}, the god of war.

micah.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|מִיכָה|tr=mīḵāh}}, shortened form of {{m|he|מִיכַיְהוּ||tr=mīḵāyᵊhū|who is like Yahweh}}.

bailey.etyRaw: {{sense|English topographic surname}} {{cln|en|surnames from Old French}} See {{m|en|bailey||outer castle wall}}

lester.etyRaw: * As an English surname, from the placename {{m|en|Leicester}}. * Also as an English surname of {{der|en|nrf|-}} origin, from {{m|en|Lestre}} in Normandy, from {{der|en|fro|Lestra}}, from {{der|en|la-med|Laxtra}}, perhaps from {{m|la|extera|t=exterior (part of a property)}}. * As an English and Scottish surname, variant of {{m|en|Lister}}. * Also as an English surname, variant of {{m|en|Laster}}. * As a Scottish and {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, shortened from {{m|en|McLester}}.

alexa.etyRaw: * From {{af|en|Alex|-a}}. A feminine form of {{m|en|Alex}}. * {{given name|en|female|clipof=Alexandra}}.

tamara.etyRaw: Of [[Slavic]] origin, mainly from {{uder|en|ru|Тама́ра}}, name of a 12th-century saint in the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], cognate with English biblical [[Tamar]], from {{uder|en|he|תמר|tr=tāmār||date palm}}.

claudia.etyRaw: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from {{borrowed|en|la|Claudia}}.

harvey.etyRaw: From ''Haerviu'', name of a Breton saint, from {{der|en|obt|hoiarn||iron}} + {{m|obt|viu||blazing}}. Cognate with modern {{cog|br|Haerviu}}. In Ireland, used as an anglicisation of {{der|en|ga|Ó hAirmheadhaigh}} and {{m|ga|Ó hEarchaidh}}. The civil parish in New Brunswick is probably named in honour of British colonial administrator {{w|John Harvey}} (1778 - 1852).

diego.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|es|Diego}}, from an Iberian {{m|la|Didacus}}, of uncertain origin.

erika.etyRaw: Spelling variant of {{m|en|Erica}}, the feminine form of {{m|en|Eric}}, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from {{der|en|non|Eiríkr}}.

genevieve.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Geneviève}} {{gloss|patron saint of Paris}}, from {{der|en|la|Genovefa}}, {{m|la|Genoveva}}, possibly either of {{der|en|gem}} origin, ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} {{af|gem-pro|*kunją|t1=kin, family|*wībą|t2=woman, wife|nocat=1}}, or of {{der|en|cel}} origin, ultimately from {{der|en|cel-pro|*genos|t=family, clan}}.

maya.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|es|maya}}, from {{der|en|yua|mayab|t=flat}} or {{der|en|yua|maaya}}, a self-designation of the northern Maya for themselves, in the form {{m|yua|maya’}} found in compounds and phrases e.g. {{m|yua|maya’ wíinik|t=Maya man}}. {{rfc|en|senses ("member or descendant of") and translation ("civilization") don't match: {{m+|fi|mayakulttuuri}} & {{m+|de|Mayakultur}} only denote the civilisation but not a person. Also, Etymology3&4 may be merged}}

miles.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|-}} given name {{m|fro|Milo}}, of problematic origin, possibly from an unknown {{der|en|gem|-}} element, or a short form of {{der|en|sla|-}} names beginning with ''mil-'' "grace, favor". The English form is associated by [[folk etymology]] with Latin {{m|la|mīles||soldier}}. As a surname, it is also derived from a {{inh|en|enm|Miles}} form of [[Michael]].

priscilla.etyRaw: Feminine diminutive form of a Roman cognomen [[Prīscus]], from {{der|en|la|prīscus||former, ancient, old-fashioned}}. Compare typologically {{m|en|Seneca}} (< {{m+|la|Seneca}} < {{m|la|senex}}).

kylie.etyRaw: {{unc|en}}, possibly from {{m|en|kylie||boomerang}}. Originally popular in [[Australia]], the name has gained popularity elsewhere in the English-speaking world due to the fame of {{w|Kylie Minogue}}. Unrelated to {{m|en|Kyle}}, though often seen as its feminine equivalent.

chester.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Chestre}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ċeaster}}, from {{m|ang|ċeaster|t=a town or city, especially a Roman one}}. The village in Nova Scotia is likely named after the city in Pennsylvania.

aidan.etyRaw: Name of an Irish saint, Anglicized from {{der|en|ga|Aodhán}} and {{der|en|gd|Aodhan}}, diminutives of {{m|ga|Aodh}} (literally "fire", the name of a [[Celtic]] sun god).

tonya.etyRaw: Phonetic rendering of {{uder|en|ru|То́ня}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Антони́на||[[Antonina]]}}.

ariana.etyRaw: Modern simplification of [[Arianna]], [[Ariane]] and [[Arianne]], all forms of the [[Greek]] name [[Ariadne]] ("most holy"; Cretan Greek ''αρι'' (ari) "most" and ''αδνος'' (adnos) "holy"). There has been some confusion with the similar sounding [[Adriana]] and [[Adrienne]]. * By [[folk etymology]] also associated with Welsh {{m|cy|arian||silver}}.

jeff.etyRaw: From {{m|en|Jeffrey}}, a variant of {{m|en|Geoffrey}}, from {{inh|en|enm|Geffrey}}, from an {{der|en|fro|-}} aristocratic name, {{m|fro|Geoffroi}} {{IPAchar|[dʒɔfreʲ]}} (> West {{ncog|frm|Geoffrey}}, East {{ncog|frm|Geoffroy}}), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in ''-us'') ''Jotfredus, Jozsfredus, Josfredus'' (10th century) and ''Jof[f]redus, Jofridus, Jaufredus'', ''Geffredus'' (11th century),<ref>Louis Guinet, ''Les emprunts gallo-romans au germanique (du 1er à la fin du Ve siècle)'', éditions Klincksieck, 1982. </ref> and ultimately of {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} origin. The second element is {{m|gem-pro|*friþuz||peace, sanctuary}}. The first element may be {{m|gem-pro|*gautaz||a [[Geat]], a [[Goth]]}} [making the Proto-Germanic term {{m|gmw-pro|*Gautafriþu}}], as opposed to {{m|gem-pro|*gōdaz||good}} or {{m|gem-pro|*gudą||god}} in ''[[Godfrey]]''; this would also make it related to {{l|en|Jocelyn}}.<ref>[[w:en:Albert Dauzat|Albert Dauzat]], ''Noms et prénoms de France'', 1951; édition revue et commentée par [[w:en:Marie-Thérèse Morlet|Marie-Thérèse Morlet]] Librairie Larousse 1980, p. 287b - 288a.</ref> <!--in the opinion of Dauzat (1951) and/or? Morlet (1980), the standard derivation is simply "a variant of Godfrey"--> The name was introduced to England by the [[Normans]] in the 11th century.

miriam.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|מִרְיָם|tr=Miryam}}, possibly from {{der|en|arc|מרים|tr=Maryām|t=bitter}}, from a root '''מר''' (''m-r'') meaning "to be bitter". The meaning of this name which is the Old Testament equivalent of {{m|en|Mary}} has been debated for centuries. Some other explanations are mutiny / rebellion / disobedience from a root '''מרי''' (''m-r-y'').

alison.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Alisoun}}, from {{der|en|fro|Alison}}, brought to England by the Normans {{gloss|from {{der|en|xno|Alison}}, from {{der|en|nrf|Alison}} }}, diminutive of {{m|fro|Aliz|}}, equivalent to English {{m|en|Alice}}, from {{der|en|goh|Adalhaid||of noble kind}}.

tanya.etyRaw: Borrowed in the twentieth century from the {{uder|en|ru|-}} pet form {{m|ru|Та́ня}} of {{m|ru|Татья́на||[[Tatiana]]}}.

duane.etyRaw: Anglicized form of the {{bor|en|ga|-}} name {{m|ga|Dubhán}} (from {{der|en|pgl|ᚇᚑᚃᚐᚌᚅᚔ}}), from {{m|ga|dubh||black, dark}}; or transferred from the surname, which is from {{der|en|ga|Ó Dubháin|lit=descendant of Dubhán}}.

maxine.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Max|-ine<id:female>}}. An English feminine form of [[Max]] coined at the end of the nineteenth century. {{piecewise doublet|en|Maxina}}.

melody.etyRaw: From the noun {{m|en|melody}}; in regular use since the 20th century.

miranda.etyRaw: {{coin|en|William Shakespeare}} for a character in ''The Tempest''; feminine of {{uder|en|la|mirandus||admirable}}.

cecil.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Caecilius}}, a Roman family name derived from {{m|la|caecus||blind}}. The surname has absorbed the {{der|en|owl|Seisyllt}}, from Latin {{m|la|Sextilius}}, from {{m|la|Sextus}}.

yolanda.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|es|Yolanda}}, the form of a medieval royal name of obscure, probably {{der|en|gem}}, origin. It has been identified with {{cog|la|Violante}} and with {{cog|grc|ἴον|t=violet}} + {{m|grc|ἄνθος|t=flower}}.

jocelyn.etyRaw: From the {{inh|en|enm|-}} male given name from {{der|en|fro|Joscelin}}, {{der|en|de|Gautzelin}}, diminutive of names beginning with the tribal name {{m|goh|Gaut|t=a [[Geat]], a [[Goth]]}}, the root form of which probably comes from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Gautalinþiz|pos=from {{com|gem-pro|*gautaz|*linþaz|nocat=1}}}}; also used as a diminutive form of the Breton name [[Josse]] (= [[Joyce]]). It survived as a surname and was revived as a given name in the nineteenth century. * Jocelyn is currently popular among U.S. Hispanics, and in the Philippines, by [[folk etymology]] explained as a feminine diminutive form of [[José]] ([[Joseph]]).

milton.etyRaw: The English place names are from {{der|en|ang|mylen||mill}} or {{m|ang|middel||middle}} + {{m|ang|tun||settlement}}.

reginald.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Reginaldus}}, Latinization of names deriving from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Raginawaldaz}}.

joanna.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

ana.etyRaw: From various languages including {{bor|en|es|-}}, {{bor|en|pt|-}}, {{bor|en|ro|-}}, {{bor|en|bg|-}}, {{bor|en|sh|-}}, {{bor|en|sl|-}}, and {{bor|en|mk|-}}, all derived{{mdash}}sometimes via {{der|en|la-lat|Anna}} in the [[Vulgate]]{{mdash}}from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἄννα||[[Anna]]}}, chiefly in reference to {{w|St Anne}} the apocryphal mother of [[Mary]] mother of [[Jesus]] but appearing in the [[New Testament]] in reference to {{w|Anna the Prophetess}}, from {{der|en|he|חַנָּה||[[Hannah]]|tr=Ḥannâ}}, from {{m|he|חַנָּה||[[grace]], [[gracious]], [[graced]] with [[child]]|tr=ḥannâ}}. As an Oregonian river, named for Ana Byars, daughter of the surveyor W.H. Byars. {{doublet|en|Ann|Anne|Anna|Hannah}}.

cecilia.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Caecilia}}, feminine form of {{m|la|Caecilius}}, a Roman family name possibly derived from the byname {{m|la|caecus|t=blind}}. Popularized by Saint Cecilia, third century Roman martyr, the patron saint of music. {{doublet|en|Sheila}}.

damian.etyRaw: From the {{uder|en|grc|-}} name {{m|grc|Δαμιανός}} which was derived from {{m|grc|δαμάω||to tame}} (see {{m|grc|δαμάζω}}). Name known in Ancient Greece, later borne by Christian saints.

aaliyah.etyRaw: Popularized by American singer Aaliyah Haughton (1979-2001). {{translit|en|ar|عَالِيَة}}.

glenda.etyRaw: Coined in the twentieth century from {{der|en|cy|glân||holy, fair}} and {{m|cy|da||good}}.

maxwell.etyRaw: From an earlier form [[Mackeswell]], meaning "Mack's well or spring", from {{inh|en|ang|welle||well}}.

hector.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Hectōr}} or {{der|en|grc|Ἕκτωρ}}, from {{m|grc|ἕκτωρ||holding fast}}, from {{m|grc|ἔχω||to have, hold}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*seǵʰ-||to hold; to overpower}}.  Sometimes used as an anglicization of various {{der|en|gd|-}} names, including {{m|gd|Eachann}} and {{m|gd|Eochaid}}. The thundercloud cluster was named by pilots during the Second World War.

jade.etyRaw: From the precious stone {{m|en|jade}}; taken into general use in the 1970s.

sidney.etyRaw: From {{der|en|ang|*Sīdaneġ}}, the name of a place in Surrey, from {{m|ang|sīd||wide}} + {{m|ang|eġ||island}}.

ada.etyRaw: Short form of {{der|en|gem}} names beginning with {{m|goh|adal||noble}}, such as [[Adelaide]]. Also Latinized form of Hebrew [[Adah]]. The programming language takes its name from [[w:Ada Lovelace|Ada Lovelace]].

lincoln.etyRaw: {{inh+|en|enm|Lincolne}}, from {{der|en|ang|Lincolle}}, {{m|ang|Lindcolen}}, {{m|ang|Lindcylene}}, from {{der|en|la|[[Lindum]] [[colōnia|Colōnia]]|t=the Roman settlement {{w|Lindum Colonia}}}}, from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*llɨnn||pool}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*lindos||lake, liquid}}, in reference to the [[w:Brayford Pool|Brayford]].  In the United States, many of the places established since 1865 are named after {{w|Abraham Lincoln}}.

roland.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|-}}, from {{der|en|frk|*Hrōþiland|lit=fame-land}}. Name of a [[paladin]] of [[Charlemagne]] in medieval French romance. {{doublet|en|Orlando}}.

bethany.etyRaw: From {{der|en|grc|Βηθανία}}, from {{der|en|arc|[[בית]] [[עניא]]|tr=beth anya|t=house of wretchedness}}.  This etymology is highly disputed; see {{w|Bethany#Bethany|Bethany}}.

ariel.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|hbo|אֲרִיאֵל|tr=ari'él|lit=lion of God|pos=a compound of {{af|he|אֲרִי|tr1=arí|gloss1=[[lion]]|אֵל|tr2=él|gloss2=[[God]]|nocat=1}}}}. * {{sense|moon of Uranus}} All of Uranus’s moons are named after characters created by {{w|William Shakespeare}} or {{w|Alexander Pope}}. The names of all four satellites of Uranus then known were suggested by {{w|John Herschel}} in 1852 at the request of {{w|William Lassell}}, though it is uncertain if Herschel devised the names, or if Lassell did so and then sought Herschel’s permission. Ariel is the name of the leading [[sylph]] in Pope’s ''{{w|The Rape of the Lock}}'' and also [[w:Ariel (The Tempest)|the spirit who serves Prospero]] in Shakespeare’s ''{{w|The Tempest}}''.

nevaeh.etyRaw: From {{m|en|heaven}}, spelled backwards. Popular since 2000 when the rock singer {{w|Sonny Sandoval}} gave the name to his baby daughter.

aurora.etyRaw: Ultimately from {{der|en|la|Aurōra}}. The Philippine placenames were {{named-after|en|occ=First Lady|Aurora Quezon|wplink=Aurora Quezon|nocap=1}}, the wife of Pres. {{w|Manuel Quezon}}, the 2nd president of the [[Philippines]].

kerry.etyRaw: * As an English surname, from a personal name derived from {{der|en|non|Kári}}. * As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Ciardha|t=descendant of Ciardha}}, from {{m|ga|ciar|t=black}}.

kendra.etyRaw: Coined in the latter half of the twentieth century, presumably a {{blend|en|Kenneth|Sandra|nocap=1}}.

clinton.etyRaw: * {{sense|English habitational surname}} A habitational surname, derived from places named {{w|lang=en|Glinton, Cambridgeshire|Glinton}} ("town on a hill") or {{w|lang=en|Glympton}} ("settlement on the River Glyme"), from {{der|en|ang|}} + {{m|ang|tun|gloss=enclosure, homestead, town}}, equivalent to the modern {{af|en|-ton}}. * {{sense|given name}} Derived from the surnames. * {{sense|DeWitt County}} Named after {{w|lang=en|DeWitt Clinton}}.

marshall.etyRaw: * As an English surname, from the noun {{m|en|marshal}}. * As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Mercier}}. * As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Marschall}}.

natasha.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ru|Ната́ша}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Ната́лья}}, cognate to [[Natalie]].

marguerite.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Marguerite}} in the 1860s. {{doublet|en|Margaret}}, ultimately from the {{der|en|grc|μαργαρίτης||pearl}}.

angelica.etyRaw: Church {{der|en|it|Angelica}}, from {{der|en|la|angelica}} or a Latinate elaboration of {{m|en|Angela}}. Name of a heroine in Ariosto's ''Orlando Furioso'' (1516).

devon.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|ang|Defenas}}, which meant both "Devonians" and "Devon," exemplifying the common [[w:Anglo-Saxons|Anglo-Saxon]] practice of naming a place after the people who inhabit it.

jenny.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Jen|y}}, historically as a [[hypochoristic]] form of {{m|en|Janet}}, {{m|en|Jane}}, etc.<ref>{{R:Etymonline|Jenny}}</ref> but now more often used as a diminutive of {{m|en|Jennifer}}. Rarely also a nickname of {{m|en|Genevieve}} (compare {{m|en|Genny}}, pronounced the same), {{m|en|Eugenia}} or {{m|en|Virginia}} (compare {{m|en|Ginny}}). {{doublet|en|Ivanka|Jan|Janelle|Janet|Janey|Janine|Jeanette|Jeanie|Jeannette|Jeannine|Jen|Jenna|Jessie|Jo|Jody|Juanita|Shanae|Sinead|Vanna}} in derivations from {{m|en|Jane}} etc. In senses related to inanimate objects, partially derived from the generic senses of {{m|en|Jane}} and partially an informal pronunciation of {{m|en|engine}}.  {{rfe|en|Source required for the claim of "engine" here.}}

bridget.etyRaw: English form of the {{der|en|ga|-}} saints' name ''[[Brighid]]'', ''[[Brigid]]''. {{doublet|en|Bride}}.

claude.etyRaw: In use from the 16th century. {{bor+|en|fr|Claude}}, from {{der|en|la|Claudius}}, the name of a Roman gens. The clan name is traditionally said to be from {{der|en|la|claudus||lame}}, but is most likely of {{der|en|sbv|-}} origin.

brendan.etyRaw: Anglicized form of the name of Irish saints, {{der|en|ga|Bréanainn}} (via {{der|en|la|Brendanus}}), from {{der|en|sga|Brénainn}}, from {{der|en|owl|breenhin|5=prince, king}}, ultimately from {{der|en|cel-pro|*brigantīnos|5=(someone) preeminent, outstanding}}, a diminutive of {{m|cel-pro|*brigantī||high, exalted}}. {{doublet|en|Brian}}.

felicia.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Felicia}}, from {{der|en|la|Fēlīcia}}, from {{m|la|fēlīcia|lit=happy things}}, the neuter plural of {{m|la|fēlīx}}, which often occurred in the phrase {{m|la|[[tempora]] fēlīcia|t=happy times}}.

guy.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|fro|Gui}}{{attn|en|borrowed directly or via Middle English?}}, from a {{der|en|frk|-}} form of {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Widō}} (compare {{der|en|odt|Wido}}<!--marking as der in case Old French borrowed it directly from there-->), a short form of names beginning with the element {{m|gmw-pro|*widu||{{l|en|wood}}}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*widuz}}; see for example modern {{cog|de|Witold}} and {{cog|osx|Widukind}}. Cognate with {{cog|it|Guido}} and thus a {{dbt|en|Guido|nocap=1}}. More at {{l|en|wood}}.

harriet.etyRaw: Anglicized form of {{der|en|fr|Henriette}}, feminine form of {{m|fr|Henri||Henry}}, popular in England in the 18th and 19th centuries.

quinn.etyRaw: The surname is {{bor+|en|ga|Ó Coinn||descendant of Chief|nocap=1}}.

geneva.etyRaw: Mentioned in {{der|en|la|-}} texts as {{m|la|Genava}}. Probably via a {{der|en|cel-pro|*genwā}} from {{der|en|ine-pro|*ǵénw-eh₂|t=knee}}, a derivative of {{m|ine-pro|*ǵónu}} in the sense of a bending river or estuary, possibly akin to {{m|en|Genoa}}.

blanche.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|fro|blanc|t=white}}. The surname originated as a nickname, or as a [[matronymic]].

velma.etyRaw: Coined at the end of the 19th century, by analogy with {{m|en|Thelma}} and {{m|en|Wilma}}.

dallas.etyRaw: # The Texas city was named after {{w|George M. Dallas}}, vice president to Polk; family name is evolved from ''dalhous'' (13th c.), meaning "dweller at the house in the dale," from {{m|en|dale}} + {{m|en|house}}. # The Scottish place-name is from {{der|en|xpi|-}}, equivalent to {{cog|cy|dôl||meadow, haugh}} + {{m|cy|gwas||abode}}.

kaleb.etyRaw: From {{der|en|he|כלב||dog}}, possibly referring to a dog’s unconditional devotion to its master.

ivy.etyRaw: From {{m|en|ivy}}, the name of a plant. An ivy branch used to be hung outside an establishment to advertise that it sold alcohol, so it may originally been an occupationational surname for the proprietor of such an establishment. {{rfv-etym|en}}

lula.etyRaw: 19th-century variant of {{m|en|Lulu}}, nickname of {{m|en|Louisa}} and {{m|en|Lucy}}. In rare cases, shortened from {{m|en|Tallulah}}.

natalia.etyRaw: {{uder|en|la|natale||birthday (of the Lord)}}, referring to birth on Christmas Day, name of an early martyr.

candace.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Candacē}}, from {{der|en|grc|Κανδάκη}}, from {{der|en|xmr|𐦲𐦷𐦲𐦡|ts=kandakə}}, a hereditary title of ancient queens of [[Napata]] (northern [[Sudan]]). <!--It said here: "The name is also associated with Late Latin {{m|la|candida||whiteness}} via {{glossary|folk etymology}}." Please source. Haven't found any evidence of this association. It also said: "The [[silent e]] at the end might be a result of this association." The final -e is already in the Latin form. Maybe it refers to the fact that this -e is not pronounced. But what does this have to do with "candida"?? Besides: If anything, I think contemporary speakers may associate it with "candy".-->

julius.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|la|Iūlius}}, of uncertain origin, possibly from {{der|en|grc|ἴουλος|t=downy first beard hairs}}, i.e. the young, or from Latin {{m|la|Jovilius|t=devoted to [[Jove]]}}. {{doublet|en|Jules}}.

payton.etyRaw: Habitational surname from a minor place in [[Sussex]], from the {{der|en|ang|-}} personal name {{m|ang|Pǣga}} + {{m|ang|tūn||enclosure; settlement, town}}.

misty.etyRaw: From the adjective {{m|en|misty}}, but sometimes also (like {{m|en|Missy}}) used as a nickname for {{m|en|Melissa}}.

mila.etyRaw: From a diminutive in many {{der|en|sla}} languages {{der|en|bg,mk,ru,sh|-}}, etc.) of female given names containing the element Mil-, -mila ("grace, beloved"), such as [[Ludmila]], [[Milena]], {{m|sh|Milica}}, and of the cognates of [[Emily]]. Also from {{bor|en|es|Mila}}.

hugh.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|fro|-}} aristocratic and saint's name {{m|fro|Hughe}}, brought to England by Normans, from a short form of {{der|en|gem|-}} names beginning with {{der|en|gem-pro|*hugiz||heart, mind}}, such as [[Hubert]]. Cognate with {{cog|ang|hyge|hyġe|mind, spirit, intellect}}. More at [[high]], [[how]].

sawyer.etyRaw: * As an English occupational surname, from {{m|en|sawyer|t=one who saws}}. Senses loaned from various languages include Jewish/{{der|en|de|Seger}} and {{m|en|Sager}}, {{der|en|sl|Žagar}}. * As a {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Seguin}}.

rosalie.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Rosalie}}, from the {{der|en|la|-}} saints’ name {{m|la|Rosālia}}, from {{m|la|rosa||rose}}. {{doublet|en|Rosalia}}.

wallace.etyRaw: An {{der|en|ang|-}} byname for a [[Welshman]] or [[Breton]], from {{der|en|xno|waleis||foreign}}; see {{m|ang|wǣlisċ}}.

bella.etyRaw: From {{der|en|it|-}}: a [[diminutive]] of [[Isabella]] and [[Arabella]], by folk etymology interpreted as {{m|it|bella||beautiful}}.

eunice.etyRaw: A biblical name from {{der|en|grc|Εὐνίκη}}, from {{com|grc|εὐ-|t1=good|νίκη|t2=victory|nocat=1}}.<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>

hilda.etyRaw: Short form of {{der|en|gem|-}} names beginning or ending in {{m|ang|hild||battle}}.

adeline.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Adeline}}, a diminutive form of {{m|en|Adela}} and {{m|en|Adele}} brought to England by the [[Norman]]s.

valeria.etyRaw: Feminine form of [[Roman]] family name {{m|la|Valerius}}, from {{der|en|la|valere|t=to be healthy, to be strong}}. {{doublet|en|Valerie}}.

nelson.etyRaw: From {{der|en|enm|-}} {{suffix|en|Neil|son}} and {{suffix|en|Nell|son}}. * In the United States, also an Anglicisation of {{der|en|gmq|-}} {{gloss|[[Scandinavian]]}} surnames such as [[Nilsen]], [[Nielsen]], and [[Nilsson]], equivalent to "son of [[Nicholas]]".

luca.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Luca}}, from {{der|en|la|Lūcās}}, from {{der|en|grc|Λουκᾶς}}, hypocoristic of {{m|grc|Λούκιος}} (from {{der|en|la|Lūcius|g=m}}) or {{m|grc|Λουκανός}} or both with {{m|grc|-ᾶς}}. As a female given name, used in {{cog|hu|-}} and {{cog|sh|-}} as an equivalent of {{m|en|Lucy}} (ultimately of same origin, from {{cog|la|Lūcia|g=f}}), but English usage is influenced by the male given name, similar {{m|en|Lucas}}, {{m|en|Luke}}, and the feminine ending {{m|en|-a}}.

dwight.etyRaw: Probably from a {{inh|en|enm|-}} female name [[Diot]], a pet form of [[Dionysia]], the feminine form of [[Dionysius]].

emmett.etyRaw: From a {{der|en|enm|-}} diminutive of the female given name [[Emma]].

antoinette.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fr|Antoinette}}, feminine diminutive of {{m|fr|Antoine}}, equivalent to {{m|en|Anthony}}.

kai.etyRaw: Taken into regular use in the 1990s, with earlier popularity peaks in Scandinavia and Germany. The medieval Danish [[Kaj]] is possibly of Roman origin, Latinized as [[Caius]], like the rare medieval English male given name [[Kay]]. The German [[#German|Kai]] may also derive from a [[West Frisian]] pet form of [[Gerard]], [[Cornelius]], [[Nicholas]], or [[Kampe]] "warrior". In the U.S. Kai has also been explained as [[Hawaiian]] {{m|haw|kai||sea}}.

lila.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Leila}} or {{m|en|Lilah}}, depending on pronunciation; also associated with {{bor|en|es|lila||lilac}}.

august.etyRaw: Early {{der|en|enm|August|August(us)}}, re-Latinized from {{der|en|ang|Agustus}}, from {{cog|la-lat|Agustus}}, from {{der|en|la|augustus||month of August}}, from the agnomen {{m|la|Augustus||venerable}} of {{w|Augustus|Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus}}, possibly from either Old Latin {{m|itc-ola|*augos|t=increase}}, from {{der|en|itc-pro|*augos}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|-}} base {{m|ine-pro|*h₂ewg-||to increase}}; or {{cog|la|avis||bird}}, referring to divination by observing bird flights, singing, feeding or entrails + {{m|la|garrio|garrīre|t=to chatter}}. {{dbt|en|august|Augustus}}.

irma.etyRaw: From {{der|en|de|Irma}} in the nineteenth century. Short form of {{der|en|gem}} names beginning with ''irm(en)-, erm(en)'' "whole, entire", from {{der|en|gem-pro|*ermunaz}}. Cognate with {{cog|en|Emma}}.

krista.etyRaw: A spelling variant of {{m|en|Christa}}, a modern short form of [[Christina]], partly borrowed from {{der|en|de|Christa}}.

shaun.etyRaw: A variant of {{m|en|Sean}}, from {{bor|en|ga|Seán}}, from {{der|en|fro|Jehan}}, from {{der|en|la|Johannes}}, variant of {{m|la|Ioannes}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννης}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָן|tr=Yōḥānān|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}. {{doublet|en|John|Jack|Johan|Johann|Johannes|Jean|Ian|Evan|Ivan|Sean|Shawn|Shane|Giovanni}} as a male name. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shauna|Sheena}} as a female name.

beulah.etyRaw: A biblical name applied to the land of Israel in Isaiah 62:4, from {{bor|en|hbo|בְּעוּלָה|tr=bəʿûlâ|t=married (woman)}}, taken up as a given name by Puritans and used figuratively for the New Earth.

virgil.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Vyrgyle}}, from {{der|en|la|Virgilius}}, from the [[Roman]] clan name {{m|la|Vergilius}}, from {{der|en|ett|-}} and of unknown meaning.

cheyenne.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Cheyenne}}, from {{der|en|dak|šahíyena}}, from {{der|en|dak|šaia|t=to speak incoherently}}, from {{der|en|dak|ša|t=red}} and {{der|en|dak|ya|t=to speak}}. <ref>{{R:OED Online|code=31490}}</ref><ref>{{cite-web|url = http://www.geocities.com/cheyenne_language/origin.htm|title = What is the origin of the word "Cheyenne"?|accessdate = September 21, 2007|date = 2002-03-03|work = Cheyenne Language Web Site|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090807032944/http://geocities.com/cheyenne_language/origin.htm|archivedate=2009-08-07}}</ref>

belinda.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Belle|inda}}, base from various Romance sources such as {{cog|fr|belle}}, {{cog|it|bella||beautiful}}, suffix Latinate form of {{cog|de|linde||soft}} (English {{m|en|linden}}, {{m|en|lithe}}). Popularised by {{w|Alexander Pope}} in his poem ''{{w|The Rape of the Lock}}'' (1714). The moon is named after a character in Pope's poem.

caden.etyRaw: Invented by American parents in the 1990s to rhyme with the equally fashionable [[Aidan]], [[Braden]], [[Hayden]] and [[Jayden]].

rowan.etyRaw: Anglicised from the {{der|en|ga|-}} saints' name {{m|ga|Ruadhán||little red one}}, or as a surname from {{m|ga|Ó Ruadháin||descendant of Ruadhán}}.

eloise.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|fr|Éloïse}}, from the {{der|en|la-med|-}} and French forms that gave rise to its [[Appendix:Glossary#doublet|doublet]] {{doublet|en|Heloise|notext=1}}.

israel.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Israel}}, from {{inh|en|ang|-}}, borrowed from {{der|en|la|Israel}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἰσραήλ}}, from {{der|en|he|יִשְׂרָאֵל||Israel|tr=yisra'él}}.<ref>{{R:Dictionary.com}}</ref><ref>{{R:MWO}}</ref> In the Bible, it is said to be from the name {{m|he|[[שרה|יִשְׂרֶה]] [[אֵל]]|tr=yisré 'él}} given to [[Jacob]] in {{R:Tanach|1|32|29}}, after which his descendants came to be known as [[Israelite]]s and their land as the "kingdom/land of Israel". The personal name, already attested in {{l+|xeb|𒅖𒊏𒅋|w=1}} (''iš-ra-il'') and {{l+|uga|𐎊𐎌𐎗𐎛𐎍|w=1}}<!-- as a personal name-->,<ref>Michael G. Hasel, ''Domination and Resistance: Egyptian Military Activity in the Southern Levant'' (Brill, 1998)</ref> has been variously translated as "he wrestles with God", "he prevails with God",<ref>James P. Boyd, ''Bible dictionary'' (Ottenheimer Publishers, 1958)</ref> or "God rules" (possibly from the same root {{m|he|ש־ר־ה}}/{{m|he|ש־ר־ר}} as {{m|he|שָׂרָה||Sarah}}).<ref>Victor P. Hamilton, ''The Book of Genesis: Chapters 18–50'' (NICOT, Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1995)</ref> [[:File:YsyriAr.gif|Line 27]] of the [[w:Merneptah Stele|Merneptah Stele]] (from about 1200 {{B.C.E.}}) is thought to contain the earliest attestation of the name ''Israel'' in any language, {{cog|egy|ysrjꜣr}}. : {{egy-h|i-i-z:Z1s*Z1s:r-i-A-r:Z1*T14-A1*B1:Z2}} {{doublet|en|Yisroel}}.

axel.etyRaw: From {{der|en|da|Aksel}}, first used for the bishop and statesman [[Absalon]] Hvide (1128–1201), from biblical [[Absalom]]. Some sources suggest that the bishop was originally named [[Áskell]], from {{der|en|non|-}} "god" + "cauldron, helmet", and Absalon was chosen as the nearest-sounding Christian equivalent, leading to the exchange of the middle consonants.

morris.etyRaw: * The surname has converged from several origins; see [[w:en:Morris (surname)#Origins|Morris]].

reagan.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{uder|en|ga|-}} Gaelic {{m|ga|Ó Riagáin|t=descendant of Riagán}}, a personal name possibly derived from {{m|ga|ríodhgach|t=impulsive, furious}}, an alternative form of [[ríogach]].

maverick.etyRaw: The surname is most famously associated with {{w|Samuel Maverick}}, a rancher from Texas who did not brand his cattle. The surname is of uncertain origin, but known to date as far back as the 1500s in [[Devon]], England.<ref>https://dn710108.ca.archive.org/0/items/mavericksofdevon00cres/mavericksofdevon00cres.pdf</ref> Its meaning is a matter of conjecture, with connections to the name {{m|en|Maurice}} being unprovable.

della.etyRaw: Possibly a variant of {{m|en|Adela}} or {{m|en|Delia}}. First appeared in the 19th century.

alberta.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Albert|a}}. The province was named after [[w:Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll|Princess Louise Caroline Alberta]].

elliott.etyRaw: English surname derived from a [[Middle English]] diminutive of ''Elie'', Old French form of [[Elias]] or [[Elijah]], meaning "my God is [[Yahweh]]". As a Scottish surname it may also represent [[Gaelic]] ''Elloch'' from a word meaning a dam or bank.

clifton.etyRaw: *Literally meaning "town by a cliff." From {{der|en|ang|clif||cliff}} + {{m|ang|tūn||town}}. Analyzable as {{suffix|en|cliff|ton}}. *In Oregon County, Missouri, from {{suffix|en|Cliff|ton}}. From being named after a {{m|en|Cliff}}, or which may be clipped to ''Clif''.

simon.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Simon}}, {{m|enm|Symond}}, {{m|enm|Symounde}}, from {{der|en|xno|Simon}}, {{m|fro|Simond}}, {{m|fro|Simund}}, a conflation of two unrelated names: one from {{der|en|la|Simon}}, from {{der|en|grc|Σίμων}}, from {{der|en|hbo|שִׁמְעוֹן||hearkening|tr=šimʿōn}}, {{doublet|en|Simeon|nocap=1}}; the other from {{der|en|non|Sigmundr}} or {{der|en|ang|Siġemund}}, both from {{der|en|gem-pro|*Sigimunduz|lit=Protector of victory}}, whence also {{m|en|Sigmund}} and {{m|en|Siegmund}}.

malcolm.etyRaw: Royal name in {{l|en|Scotland}}, anglicised from various historical {{der|en|cel-gae}} names equivalent to {{der|en|gd|maol|Maol}} {{m|gd|Chaluim}} or {{m|gd|Calum}}, {{der|en|ga|maol|Maol}} {{m|ga|Colm}}, {{der|en|mga|Máel Coluim}}, {{der|en|sga|[[Máel]] [[Columb]]|lit=devotee of [Saint] [[Columba]]}}; proper nouns derived from {{m|sga|máel|t=tonsured}} from {{der|en|cel-pro|*mailos}}, and {{m|sga|columb|t=dove}} from {{der|en|la|columbus}}.<ref>Patrick Hanks and Flavia Hodges: A Concise Dictionary of First Names. Oxford University Press 2001.</ref>

verna.etyRaw: Coined in the 19th century, from {{der|en|la|vernus||spring-like}} or as a feminine of {{m|en|Vernon}}.

inez.etyRaw: Anglicised form of {{bor|en|es|Inés}} and {{bor|en|pt|Inês}}, both from  {{der|en|la|Agnes}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἁγνή}}. First used in 18th century English poetry and plays referring to [[w:Inês de Castro|Inês de Castro]]. {{dbt|en|Agnes}}.

kent.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|cel-bry-pro}} {{inh+|en|enm|Kent}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Cent}}, from {{der|en|la|Cantium}}, from {{der|en|cel-bry|-}} {{m|cel-bry-pro|*Cantio}} (compare {{cog|sga|céite||gathering, folkmoot, hillock}}), from {{der|en|cel-pro|*kantos||corner, rim}}.

carly.etyRaw: A feminine form of {{m|en|Carl}} with {{affix|en|-y<id:diminutive>}}, taken to use in the latter half of the 20th century; also a pet form of {{m|en|Carla}}, {{m|en|Carlene}} and {{m|en|Carlotta}}.

braxton.etyRaw: Perhaps a habitational surname from the village of {{m|en|Branxton}}, in [[Northumberland]].

beau.etyRaw: Shortened from surname type given names such as [[Beauregard]] or [[Beaumont]], or from the {{uder|en|fr|-}} word {{m|fr|beau}}.

dillon.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{der|en|br|Leon}} and {{der|en|nrf|Léon}}, named after Sir Henry de Leon of the {{w|Viscounty of Léon}}.<ref>Grenham, John (1994). The Little Book of Irish Clans. Dublin, Ireland: John Hinde. p. 19.</ref> Related to the surname {{m|en|Lyon}}. Unrelated to the name {{m|en|Dylan}}, although the homophony may result in the two being considered variant spellings of the same name.

sonya.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ru,uk|Со́ня}}, an informal pet form of {{m|ru|Со́фья}}, {{m|uk|Софі́я}} or {{m|ru|Софи́я||Sofia, Sophia}}, from the {{der|en|grc|σοφία||wisdom}}. It was introduced into English through 19th century Russian literature and taken into general use in early twentieth century.

malachi.etyRaw: From {{der|en|la|Mālāchiās}}, from {{der|en|grc|Μαλαχίας}}, from {{der|en|he|מַלְאָכִי|tr=mal'achi, malʼāḵî|lit=my messenger}}, singular form of {{m|he|מַלְאָךְ|tr=mal'akh|gloss=[[angel]]; [[messenger]]; [[ambassadors]]}} with first-person singular personal pronoun as possessor.

abel.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Abel}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Ābel}}, from {{der|en|la|Abel}}, from {{der|en|grc|Ἅβελ}}, from {{der|en|hbo|הֶבֶל||Abel|tr=Héḇel}}, possibly from the homonymous word {{m|hbo|הֶבֶל||breath, vapor; vanity|tr=heḇel}} or from {{der|en|akk|𒌉𒍑|tr=ablu|t=son}}.

paisley.etyRaw: From {{der|en|gd|Pàislig||pasture}}. Despite occasional respellings such as {{m|en||Paisleigh}}, this word does not etymologically contain the suffix {{m|en|-ley}}/{{m|en|-leigh}}.

valentina.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|es|-}}, {{bor|en|it|-}}, and {{bor|en|la|Valentīna}}, feminine forms of {{der|en|es|-}} and {{der|en|it|Valentino}}, and {{der|en|la|Valentīnus<id:cognomen>}}. {{doublet|en|Valentine|Valentinus|Valentino|Valentini}}.

cassidy.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, Anglicized from {{m|ga|Ó Caiside|t=descendant of Caiside}}, from {{m|ga|cas|t=curly-haired}}.

reese.etyRaw: * As a given name and British surname generally from {{der|en|cy|Rhys|lit=ardor}}. * Chiefly in North America, the surname may also be from unrelated {{der|en|de|Reese|lit=giant}}.

emery.etyRaw: From medieval Germanic personal names, either a variant of [[Amory]], from {{m|und||Amalric}}, {{der|en|gem-pro|*amal||vigor, bravery}} (compare {{m|gem-pro|*ammōną}}) + {{der|en|goh|rīhhi||ruler}}, or of [[Henry]], from {{der|en|goh|Heimrich}}, from {{m|goh|heim||home}} + {{m|goh|rīhhi||ruler}}.

yvette.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|fr|Yvette}}. The politics sense is a reference to the name of a docile young girl in a school textbook, and was popularized by separatist politician {{w|Lise Payette}} (1931–2018).

myra.etyRaw: First used by the poet Fulke Greville, possibly as an [[anagram]] of [[Mary]].

jasper.etyRaw: A name given to one of the [[Magi]] in a medieval European cult, from {{cog|hbo|גִּזְבָּר|tr=gizbar}}, ultimately from {{der|en|xme-old|*ganǰabarah}}; see it for more.

ira.etyRaw: From a {{der|en|he|-}} name {{m|he|עִירָא|tr='ira}}, from a word meaning "watchful".

mya.etyRaw: A modern phonetic spelling of {{m|en|Maia}} or {{m|en|Maya}}.

olga.etyRaw: Borrowed in the 19th century from {{der|en|orv|О́льга}}, name of a Kievan [[knyaginya]] ({{w|Saint Olga of Kiev}}), a medieval form of [[Helga]], {{der|en|non|heilagr||holy; inviolable, sacred}}. {{doublet|en|Helga}}.

otis.etyRaw: A [[Appendix:Glossary#patronymic|patronymic]] surname derived from {{inh|en|enm|-}} genitive case of the {{der|en|gem|-}} given name ''Ote, Ode'', cognate to modern {{m|en|Otto}}.

donovan.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|ga|Ó Donndubháin||descendant of (a person named) brown & black}}, from {{m|ga|donn||brown}} and {{m|ga|dubh||black}}.

graham.etyRaw: The surname derives from ''[[Grantham|Gra(nt)ham]]'', the name of a place in [[Lincolnshire]], from {{inh|en|ang|*grand||gravel}} + {{m|ang|hām||homestead}}.

gage.etyRaw: An [[occupational]] surname from {{der|en|enm|gage|gage, guage|measure}} for an [[assayer]], or {{m|enm|gage||pledge}} for a moneylender.

mallory.etyRaw: From an {{der|en|xno|-}} nickname for an unfortunate person, from {{der|en|fro|maleure}}, {{m|fro|malheure||unhappy, unlucky}}<ref>{{R:en:DAFN}}</ref> (whence {{cog|fr|malheur}}), from {{af|fro|mal|t1=bad|eur|t2=fortune|nocat=1}}.

selena.etyRaw: Either a variant of {{m|en|Selina}}, from {{der|en|la|Caelīna||heavenly|pos=from {{m|la|caelum||sky, heaven}}}}, or from {{m|en|Selene}}, the {{der|en|grc|-}} goddess of the moon.

lucia.etyRaw: [[Latinate]] variant of {{m|en|Lucy}}, or today borrowed from modern Italian. Name of a Sicilian martyr, {{uder|en|la|Lūcia}}, feminine form of the Roman [[praenomen]] {{m|la|Lūcius}}.

tabitha.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|arc|sc=Hebr|טביתא|tr=Ṭabītā’||doe, roe, gazelle}}, translated as [[Dorcas]] in the Bible.

leland.etyRaw: Shortened from {{m|en|McLeland}}, {{m|en|McClellan}}, from {{bor|en|ga|Mac}} {{m|ga|giolla|Giolla}} {{m|ga|Fhaoláin}}, "son of servant of (Saint) {{m|ga|Faolán}} (=Little Wolf)".

trenton.etyRaw: Originally named "Trent's town" in the 17th century, after a [[Quaker]], William [[Trent]]. The town in Nova Scotia is named after the capital of New Jersey.

colby.etyRaw: From either the {{der|en|non|-}} personal name {{m|non|Koli}} or {{m|non|kol||charcoal}} + {{m|non|býr||settlement}}.

hubert.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fro|Hubert}}, ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|*hugiz|t=mind}} + {{m|gem-pro|*berhtaz|t=bright, famous}}. See {{w|Saint Hubert}}.

ellis.etyRaw: * As an English surname, from the {{der|en|enm|-}} personal name {{m|enm|Elis}}, an {{der|en|fro|-}} form of {{m|en|Elias}}. Compare {{m|en|Elijah}}, {{m|en|Lias}}, {{m|en|Ely}}. Also sometimes from the {{m|enm|Elice}}, a pet form of {{m|en|Elizabeth}}. * As a {{der|en|cy|-}} surname, shortened from the personal name {{m|cy|Elisse}}, {{m|cy|Elisedd}}, from the archaic {{m|cy|elus|t=benevolent, kind}}.

archie.etyRaw: {{clipping|en|Archibald}} {{suffix|en||ie<id:diminutive>}}. The sense “anti-aircraft artillery” is said to be from airmen dodging hostile fire and shouting “Archibald, certainly not”, the refrain of a then popular music hall song of the same name first performed by {{w|George Robey}} in 1911.<ref>{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary|entry=Archibald}}</ref><ref>{{cite-web|date=6 June 2017|author=Julian Walker|title=Archibald? Certainly not!|work=Languages and the First World War|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806024104/https://languagesandthefirstworldwar.wordpress.com/2017/06/06/archibald-certainly-not/}}</ref><ref name="Air of Authority">{{cite-web|author=M B Barrass|date=17 April 2002|title=Air Vice-Marshal A E Borton|work=Air of Authority - A History of RAF Organisation|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20020712205857/https://www.rafweb.org/Biographies/Borton.htm}}</ref><ref name="Mental Floss">{{cite-web|author=Paul Anthony Jones|date=7 August 2014|title=21 Slang Terms From World War I|work=w:Mental Floss|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810212339/https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/58233/21-slang-terms-world-war-i}}</ref> This habit probably originated with the pilot and commander {{w|Amyas Borton}} (1886–1969).<ref name="Air of Authority"/><ref name="Mental Floss"/>

lana.etyRaw: Short form of {{m|en|Alana}}, or from {{bor|en|ru|Ла́на}}, diminutive of several names including {{m|ru|Светла́на}}.

alfredo.etyRaw: From [[w:Alfredo alla Scrofa|Alfredo alla Scrofa]], an Italian restaurant in [[Rome]] where the pasta dish [[fettuccine Alfredo]] was originally served, named after its founder Alfredo Di Lelio. {{doublet|en|Alfred}}.

zane.etyRaw: * The usage seems to date from the American writer Zane Grey (1875-1939), born Pearl Zane Gray. It was the surname of his mother's family, of unknown meaning. * Sometimes explained as a form of {{m|en|John}} because of the resemblance to {{m|en|Shane}}, or because Italian surnames such as {{m|it|Zanelli}} and {{m|it|Zanetto}} derive from the equivalent name {{m|it|Giovanni}}. * In some cases, a respelling of {{m|en|Zayn}}, which is of {{der|en|ar|-}} origin.

wilbur.etyRaw: From an {{inh|en|ang|-}} female given name {{m|ang|Wilburg}}, from {{m|ang|wil||will}} + {{m|ang|burh||fortress}}.

anastasia.etyRaw: From the name of a 4th-century martyr, {{translit|en|grc|Ἀναστασία|notext=1}}, from {{m|grc|ἀνάστασις||resurrection}}. The name, and its male counterpart [[Anastasius]], were originally given to children who were born around Eastertime during the early years of Christianity.

jude.etyRaw: Short form of {{m|en|Judas}}, used in an attempt to distinguish the [[Apostle]] ''Judas Thaddaeus'' from ''Judas Iscariot''.<ref> A Dictionary of First Names (OUP)</ref> From Old Testament {{m|en|Judah}}, {{der|en|he|יְהוּדָה|tr=yehudá}}, said to mean “praised”.

estelle.etyRaw: {{dercat|en|itc-pro}} {{bor+|en|fr|Estelle}}, from {{der|en|oc|estela||star}}, from {{der|en|la|stēlla}}. {{doublet|en|étoile|estoile|stella|stelo}}. Name of a third century martyr.

celia.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|la|Caelia}}, feminine of Roman family name {{m|la|Caelius}}, probably from {{m|la|caelum||heaven}}. Introduced into English by [[w:William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]] in ''As You Like It''.

waylon.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Wayland}} popularized by the American singer {{w|Waylon Jennings}} who was originally named Wayland.

bernadette.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|fr|Bernadette}}, made famous by St. Bernadette of Lourdes.

aimee.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|fr|Aimée||beloved}}. A variation of the English {{m|en|Amy}}.

emanuel.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Emmanuel}}, borrowed from {{der|en|es|-}} and from various other European languages.

london.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Londoun}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Lunden}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|-}} via {{der|en|la|Londinium}} – see for details. {{doublet|en|Londinium}}.

forrest.etyRaw: English surname, from the noun {{m|en|forest}}. Also adopted and translated from the word for "forest" in various other languages by settlers.

geoffrey.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Geffrey}}, from an {{der|en|fro|-}} aristocratic name, {{m|fro|Geoffroi}} {{IPAchar|[dʒɔfreʲ]}} (> West {{ncog|frm|Geoffrey}}, East {{ncog|frm|Geoffroy}}), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in ''-us'') ''Jotfredus, Jozsfredus, Josfredus'' (10th century) and ''Jof[f]redus, Jofridus, Jaufredus'', ''Geffredus'' (11th century),<ref>Louis Guinet, ''Les emprunts gallo-romans au germanique (du 1er à la fin du Ve siècle)'', éditions Klincksieck, 1982. </ref> and ultimately of {{der|en|gem-pro|-}} origin. The second element is {{m|gem-pro|*friþuz|t=peace, sanctuary}}. The first element may be {{m|gem-pro|*gautaz|t=a [[Geat]], a [[Goth]]}} [making the Proto-Germanic term {{m|gmw-pro|*Gautafriþu}}, as opposed to {{m|gem-pro|*gōdaz|t=good}} or {{m|gem-pro|*gudą|t=god}} in ''[[Godfrey]]''; this would also make it related to {{l|en|Jocelyn}}].<ref>{{w|Albert Dauzat}}, ''Noms et prénoms de France'', 1951; édition revue et commentée par {{w|Marie-Thérèse Morlet}}, Librairie Larousse, 1980, p. 287b - 288a.</ref> <!--in the opinion of Dauzat (1951) and/or? Morlet (1980), the standard derivation is simply "a variant of Godfrey"--> The name was introduced to England by the [[Normans]] in the 11th century. Partially displaced {{ncog|ang|Ceolfriþ}}.

johanna.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Johanna}}, variant of {{m|la|Joanna}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena|Zhanna}}.

horace.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|la|Horatius}}, a Roman family name of obscure origin, possibly from {{der|en|ett|-}}. {{doublet|en|Horatio}}.

darius.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|Dārīus}}, from {{der|en|grc|Δᾱρεῖος}}, from {{der|en|peo|𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎢𐏁|tr=Dārayauš}}, shortened form of {{m|peo|𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎺𐎢𐏁|tr=Dārayavaʰuš}}; see there for more.

wendell.etyRaw: Short form of {{uder|en|gem|-}} compound names beginning with the tribal name ''Wendel-'', "a [[Wend]]".

zion.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|Sion}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Syon}}, from {{der|en|la-ecc|Sīōn}}, from {{der|en|grc-koi|Σῑών}}, from {{der|en|hbo|צִיּוֹן|tr=ṣiyyôn}}. Initial {{m|en||Z-}} was likely under influence from {{der|en|de-ear|Zion}}, itself influenced by the {{w|Ashkenazi}} pronunciation {{IPAchar|/t͡s/}}.

michaela.etyRaw: From {{suffix|en|Michael|a}}. Latinate feminine form of {{m|en|Michael}}, first appearing as an [[Appendix:Glossary#anglicisation|anglicisation]] of the {{der|en|pt|Micaela|("Micaela")}} and {{der|en|es|Micaela|("Micaela")}}. {{doublet|en|Michelle}}.

amari.etyRaw: The surname is of multiple origins, including: * A variant of {{m|en|Amaro}}, from {{der|en|it|Amaro}}. * A variant of {{m|en|Amar}}, from {{der|en|ar|عَمَّار}}. See also {{doublet|en|Umari|Umar|Omar|Amar|notext=1}}. * A Japanese surname ultimately deriving from {{bor|en|ja|余り|tr=amari||remainder, surplus}}.

grady.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from {{m|ga|Ó Grádaigh}} (see {{m|en|O'Grady}}) or {{m|ga|Mag Bhrádaigh}} (see {{m|en|McGrady}}).

lane.etyRaw: As an English surname, from {{m|en|lane}}; as an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, from several origins, including {{m|ga|Laighin}}.  See [[w:Lane (surname)|Lane]].

kelvin.etyRaw: Of {{der|en|cel|-}}/{{der|en|gd|-}} origin, possibly from {{m|gd|caol||narrow}} or {{m|gd|coille||wooded}} + {{m|gd|abhainn||river}}.  The surname is derived from the river. The surname was also possibly influenced by {{m|en|Calvert}} ({{cog|enm|calfhirde}}).

trent.etyRaw: {{swp|River +}} {{inh+|en|enm|Trent}}, from {{inh|en|ang|Trēonte}}; Koch (2006) derives the river name from {{der|en|cel-pro|*tri-sent(o)-on-ā-}}, from the elements {{m|cel-pro|*trei||through}} + {{m|cel-pro|*sentus||path}}. Traditionally said to be from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|-}} elements equivalent to {{m|cy|tros||over}} + {{m|cy|hynt||way}}, often taken to mean "the {{l|en|trespasser}}" The surname in some cases is a shortening of "{{m|en|Tranent}}", or "{{m|en|Tranant}}" in {{der|en|gd|-}}, a geographical location in {{l|en|East Lothian}}. "Tranant" itself is possibly of {{m|en|Brythonic}} {{gloss|{{der|en|cel|-}}}} origin.

esmeralda.etyRaw: From {{der|en|es|esmeralda||emerald}}, as first used in the novel ''[[w:The Hunchback of Notre Dame|Notre-Dame de Paris]]'' (1831) by [[w:Victor Hugo|Victor Hugo]].

hayley.etyRaw: Localities in England, from {{inh|en|ang|-}} {{m|ang|hēg||hay}} + {{m|ang|lēah||wood, clearing}}. Equivalent to {{suf|en|hay|-leigh|alt2=-ley|t2={{l|en|lea}}}}.

julianna.etyRaw: Modern combination of {{compound|en|Julie|Anna}}, perhaps sometimes intended as a form of {{m|en|Juliana}}.<ref>{{R:en:DFN|page=151|column=1}}</ref>

henrietta.etyRaw: Latinate form of {{der|en|fr|Henriette}}, derived from the male [[given name]] {{m|en|Henry}}.

alaina.etyRaw: A variant of {{m|en|Alana}} coined in the 20th century from {{m|fr|Alain}}, the French equivalent of {{m|en|Alan}}.

sallie.etyRaw: A less common spelling of [[Sally]]; see {{m|en|-ie}}.

may.etyRaw: From {{inh|en|enm|May}}, {{m|enm|Mai}}, from {{der|en|fro|mai}}, from {{der|en|la|Maius||Maia's month}}, from {{m|la|Maia}}, a Roman earth goddess.

corinne.etyRaw: From the {{der|en|fr|-}} equivalent of ''[[Corinna]]'', from {{der|en|grc|κόρη||girl, maiden, daughter}}.

khloe.etyRaw: Variant of {{m|en|Khloé}}, a fanciful spelling variant of {{m|en|Chloe}}, made known in the 2000s by American TV personality {{w|Khloé Kardashian}}.

gael.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|ga|Gael}}, alt. {{m|ga|Gaol}}, from earlier {{m|gd|Gaoidheal}}, cognate with Scottish Gaelic {{m|gd|Gàidheal}} and Manx ''Gael'', from {{der|en|mga|Gaídel}}, from {{der|en|sga|Goídel||Irishman}}, a loanword from {{der|en|owl|Guoidel||wild man, warrior}} (also recorded as a personal name in the {{w|Book of Llandaff}}), from {{der|en|cel-bry-pro|*Guɨðel||savage, woodsman}}, from {{der|en|cel-pro|*weidelos||savage, woodsman}}, related to {{m|cel-pro|*weidus|t=wild}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₁weydʰh₁-||wood, wilderness}} (cf. {{cog|ang|wāþ||hunt}}).{{ref|{{R:cel:Matasovic 2009|page=408}}}} {{doublet|en|Goidel}}. {{false cognate|en|Gaul,Gallia}}. Medieval Irish traditions, including the ''{{w|Lebor Gabála Érenn}}'', trace the origin of the Goídels to an eponymous ancestor, {{w|Goídel Glas}}, but this is no longer held to be the ultimate etymology of the word.

salvador.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|es,pt|Salvador}}, chiefly various placenames honoring {{w|Jesus Christ}}, from {{der|en|es,pt|salvador||[[savior]]}}, from {{der|en|la|salvator}}, from {{m|la|salvo|salvāre|to [[save]]}} + {{m|la|-tor|pos=forming [[agent noun]]s}}. In Spanish placenames, frequently a clipping of {{der|en|es|San Salvador||[[holy|Holy]] [[savior|Savior]]}}. {{doublet|en|savior|Salvator|Salvatore}}.

rory.etyRaw: Anglicized form of {{der|en|gd|Ruairidh}} and {{der|en|ga|Ruairí||red-haired king}}, from {{der|en|sga|Ruaidrí||red king}}.

nettie.etyRaw: Suffixed with {{af|en|-ie<id:diminutive>}}, compare {{m|en|Neddie}} and {{m|en|Nellie}}, respectively from {{m|en|Edward}} and {{m|en|Eleanor}}.

orlando.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|it|Orlando||Roland}}, ultimately from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*Hrōþiland}}. The city in Florida has gone by the name since 1857, perhaps in honor of the soldier [[w:Orlando Reeves|Orlando Reeves]], whom the {{l|en|Seminole}}s killed there in 1835. Previously, it had been settled in 1844 as {{l|en|Jernigan}}.<ref name=Etymonline>{{R:Etymonline}}</ref> {{doublet|en|Roland}}.

tyson.etyRaw: * A variant of {{m|en|Tison}}. A nickname from {{der|en|fro|tison||firebrand}}. * A {{l|en|patronymic}} English surname, variant of {{m|en|Dyson}}, from {{suffix|en|Dennis|son}}. * In the US, adopted by a German family who came to America (Germantown, PA) in 1683, originally named {{der|en|de|Teisen}} "son of {{m|de|Theiss}}", which was short for {{m|de|Matthias}}. Original spellings were {{m|de|Theisen}}, {{m|de|Theissen}}, {{m|de|Teisen}}, {{m|de|Teison}}.

ty.etyRaw: {{clipping|en|[[Tyrone]], [[Tyler]], [[Tyson]], [[Tyron]], and other male given names beginning with "Ty"}}.

carolina.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|it|Carolina}} or its etymon {{bor|en|la|Carolīna}}, from {{m|la|Carolus|t=Charles}} + {{m|la|-īna|pos=feminine diminutive suffix}}.<ref>{{R:en:DFN|page=48|column=1}}</ref> {{surf|en|Carol|pos1=male given name|-ina|pos2=feminine diminutive suffix|nocat=1}}. {{doublet|en|Caroline}}. The U.S. states are named for {{w|Charles I of England}}.

ashlyn.etyRaw: An anglicized form of {{der|en|ga|Aisling||dream, vision}} with {{affix|en|-lyn}}.

elisabeth.etyRaw: The spelling of {{m|en|Elizabeth}} used in the [[Authorized Version]] of the New Testament. Borrowed from {{der|en|grc|Ἐλισάβετ}}, a transliteration of {{der|en|he|אֱלִישֶׁבַע|tr=Elishéva|t=my [[God]] is an oath}}.

jana.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|cs|Jana}}, ultimately from {{der|en|grc-koi|Ἰωάννα}}, from {{der|en|he|יוֹחָנָה|tr=Yôḥānāh|lit=[[God]] is [[gracious]]}}, the feminized form of {{m|he|יְהוֹחָנָן|tr=Yəhōḥānān}} which produced {{m|en|John}} and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of {{m|en|John}} and {{m|en|Jack}} and earlier use of {{m|en|Joan}} in the same role. {{doublet|en|Ivana|Jane|Janice|Janis|Jean|Jeanne|Jen|Joan|Joanna|Joanne|Johanna|Juana|Shavonne|Sian|Siobhan|Shane|Shaun|Shauna|Sheena}}.

sage.etyRaw: * As an English and {{der|en|fr|-}} surname, from {{m|en|sage|id=wise person}}, a nickname for a wise person. The given name, in general use since the 1990s, is also associated with the {{l|en|sage|id=Salvia officinalis}} plant. Compare {{m|en|Desage}}, {{m|en|Lesage}}. * As an {{der|en|ga|-}} surname, variant of {{m|en|Savage}}. * As a {{der|en|de|-}} surname, from a placename derived from the noun {{m|de|sege|t=sedge}} (see {{m|en|sedge}}).

mariana.etyRaw: Latinized form of {{m|en|Marian}}, ultimately from {{m|en|Mary}} or {{m|en|Mary}} + {{m|en|Ann}}. It is also the feminine form of {{der|en|la|Mariānus}}, derivative of {{m|la|Marius}}, but these rather rare Roman names have been completely intertwined with {{m|en|Maria}} in the Christian era.

mona.etyRaw: Anglicized from {{bor|en|ga|-}} and {{bor|en|gd|Muadhnait}}, from {{der|en|mga|múad|t=noble}}. In northern Europe, where the name is much more popular, Mona is interpreted as a diminutive of {{m|en|Monica}} or, rarely, of {{m|en|Ramona}}, and sometimes associated with the title of da Vinci's painting ''Mona (=[[madonna]]) Lisa''. The Arabic and Persian name {{l|ar|مُنىٰ}} is sometimes Romanised as [[Mona]].

alina.etyRaw: {{bor+|en|it|Alina}}, or a Latinate form of {{bor|en|fr|Aline}}, ultimately from diminutives of the same Germanic name {{m|en|Adela}}, {{m|en|Adele}}.

leigh.etyRaw: From the nominative case of {{inh|en|ang|lēah||wood, meadow}}, 'dweller by the wood or clearing'.

dixie.etyRaw: {{etydate|1859}}. {{unk|en}}, but may come from the [[Mason-Dixon line|Mason-'''Dixon''' line]], the boundary between the northern states and the southern states, or from the slang term {{m|en|dixie}} for a Louisiana $10 bill (equivalent to English ''[[tenner]]''), in turn from French {{m|fr|dix}} (ten).<ref>Funk, W. J., ''Word origins and their romantic stories'', New York, Wilfred Funk, Inc.</ref>

lorena.etyRaw: From {{uder|en|it|-}} and {{uder|en|es|-}}, by [[folk etymology]] associated with [[Laura]]. Henry Webster's title for his song was inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's [[Lenore]].

cleo.etyRaw: Shortened from {{m|en|Cleopatra}} or a variant of {{m|en|Clio}}. The rare male name derives from names of Ancient Greek origin such as {{m|en|Cleon}} and ''Cleopas''.

ora.etyRaw: * {{sense|given name}} First appeared in the 19th century when similar sounding names like {{m|en|Cora}}, {{m|en|Dora}} and {{m|en|Nora}} were in fashion. Possibly shortened from {{m|en|Aurelia}}, sometimes spelled {{m|en|Ora Lee}}, or, {{m|en|Aura Lea}}, in the American civil war song. * {{sense|Italian commune}} Borrowed from {{bor|en|it|Ora}}

ali.etyRaw: From {{bor|en|ar|عَلِيّ|lit=high, exalted}}, from the [[Arabic]] root {{ar-root|ع ل ي|nocat=1}}.

noelle.etyRaw: From {{der|en|fr|Noëlle}}, the feminine form of the male given name {{m|fr|Noël}}.

effie.etyRaw: From {{affix|en|Euphemia|-ie|id2=diminutive}}, or, very rarely, from modern Greek [[Eftychia]] or [[Euthemia]] (diminutive form).

irving.etyRaw: Variant of the Scottish habitational surname {{m|en|Irvine}}, probably from a {{der|en|cel|-}} word cognate with {{cog|cy|ir}}, {{m|cy|yr||fresh}} + {{m|cy|afon||river}}.

sylvester.etyRaw: Borrowed from {{bor|en|la|sylvester||woody, rural}} from {{m|la|silva||wood}}; name of a [[saint]] whose [[feast day]] falls on December 31.

kyla.etyRaw: Modern invention that can be explained as a feminine form of {{m|en|Kyle}} with {{affix|en|-a}}.
